t: vulnerability-lookup: 2FA Disabled via Unauthenticated GET Request and Unpublished Comments Accessible Without Authorization
d: vulnerability-lookup prior to version 7.1.0 contains two security issues in its web interface. First, the /user/toggle_2fa endpoint accepted HTTP GET requests and disabled the authenticated user's two-factor authentication without requiring password confirmation. Because the state-changing operation was reachable via GET, an attacker with a basic account could embed an image element (or any other GET-triggering markup) in a comment pointing to that endpoint. When a victim with 2FA enabled viewed the comment, their browser silently issued the GET request, disabling the victim's second factor of authentication. No CSRF token was enforced on the GET path, and no password was required to confirm the action. Second, the comment detail page (/comment/<uuid>) rendered unpublished comments to any visitor who possessed the URL, bypassing the moderation workflow that was intended to keep such content hidden until approved. The API correctly restricted access, but the web view did not enforce the same authorization check. The combined effect allows an attacker to degrade a victim's account security (removal of 2FA) through a single page view and to read content that was not yet approved for public release.

t: Matthias-Wandel jhead PNG Section pngfile.c RemovePngSection double free
d: A security vulnerability has been detected in Matthias-Wandel jhead up to 3.3. This affects the function RemovePngSectionByType/RemovePngSection of the file src/pngfile.c of the component PNG Section Handler. The manipulation leads to double free. Remote exploitation of the attack is possible. The exploit has been disclosed publicly and may be used. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

t: io_uring/io-wq: save worker type before dropping its reference
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring/io-wq: save worker type before dropping its reference io_wq_cancel_tw_create() inspects cb->func after calling io_worker_cancel_cb(). For an existing worker, that call can drop the last worker reference and wake io_worker_exit(). If the canceling task is preempted, the worker can be unlinked and freed by kfree_rcu() before the callback function is inspected. KASAN reports a slab-use-after-free read in this path. Save whether the callback belongs to an unpublished continuation worker while its reference is still held, then use the saved result for the conditional free. This preserves the existing accounting and frees only the worker allocated for the canceled continuation.

t: io_uring/net: mask socket type with SOCK_TYPE_MASK in io_socket_bpf_populate()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring/net: mask socket type with SOCK_TYPE_MASK in io_socket_bpf_populate() When an IORING_OP_SOCKET request is prepared in io_socket_prep(), sock->type retains creation flags such as SOCK_CLOEXEC and SOCK_NONBLOCK until __sys_socket_file() masks them off with SOCK_TYPE_MASK during execution. However, io_socket_bpf_populate() copies sock->type into bctx->socket.type without masking off ~SOCK_TYPE_MASK. As a result, a cBPF filter inspecting bctx->socket.type against socket types such as SOCK_DGRAM or SOCK_STREAM can be bypassed by ORing SOCK_CLOEXEC or SOCK_NONBLOCK into the socket type. Mask sock->type with SOCK_TYPE_MASK when populating bctx->socket.type.

t: io_uring/register: enforce per-task restrictions in io_uring_register_blind()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring/register: enforce per-task restrictions in io_uring_register_blind() When io_uring_register(2) is invoked with fd == -1, it dispatches directly to io_uring_register_blind() without checking current->io_uring_restrict. As a result, a task with per-task register restrictions installed via IORING_REGISTER_RESTRICTIONS can still invoke blind registration opcodes such as IORING_REGISTER_SEND_MSG_RING even when those opcodes are not in the task's allowed register_op bitmap. Check current->io_uring_restrict->register_op in io_uring_register_blind() before dispatching blind registration opcodes.

t: io_uring/bpf-ops: clear bpf_ctx while submitting SQEs
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring/bpf-ops: clear bpf_ctx while submitting SQEs bpf_io_uring_submit_sqes() calls io_submit_sqes() from inside the loop program, with current->bpf_ctx set, and requests issued inline run with it set too. The socket code uses has_current_bpf_ctx() to recognize calls from bpf_setsockopt() and friends, where the caller holds the socket lock and has already been vetted, and skips both. So a SOCKET_URING_OP_SETSOCKOPT from the SQ passes sockopt_capable() without the capability, and runs without lock_sock(). A task with no capability can set SO_MARK, IP_TRANSPARENT or TCP_REPAIR, and two threads changing IP_OPTIONS on one socket, one through the ring, double free in no time. SOCK_DESTROY via IORING_OP_SENDMSG ends up in tcp_abort() without the lock the same way. Clear the run context around io_submit_sqes(). The SQEs come from userspace and must be issued like those of any other ring. They still run inside the program's RCU tasks trace read section, so a request that sleeps there holds up that grace period, but other request types do that already.

t: io_uring: free the task context after a grace period
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring: free the task context after a grace period A task other than the owner can free a request, io_ring_exit_work() running the local task_work of a DEFER_TASKRUN ring for example, or io_do_iopoll() reaping completions. io_put_task() then takes the else branch: percpu_counter_sub(&tctx->inflight, 1); if (unlikely(atomic_read(&tctx->in_cancel))) wake_up(&tctx->wait); put_task_struct(tctx->task); The first line is what lets the owner leave io_uring_cancel_generic(), and on exec it frees the tctx right after. Nothing holds that off for the remaining three lines, the task reference only covers a tctx freed along with the task_struct. It used to work out because io_uring_del_tctx_node() took the uring_lock that the freeing side holds across io_put_task(), until that moved to tctx_lock. Free the tctx with kfree_rcu(), and enter an RCU read section in io_put_task() before the count is dropped.

t: io_uring/sqpoll: don't wait for the thread to exit
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring/sqpoll: don't wait for the thread to exit io_sq_thread_stop() wakes the SQPOLL thread and waits for it to exit. The thread belongs to the thread group that created the ring, so a SIGSTOP or the cgroup freezer holds it in get_signal(), and the wake up doesn't change that. io_ring_exit_work() then sleeps in that wait until someone continues or kills the process. iou_exit has 64 slots, so 64 closed SQPOLL rings of a stopped process keep every other ring from being freed, for everyone. Don't wait. Set the stop bit, wake the thread, and let it exit when it gets to run again. The sqd can now outlive its last ring, so give it a second refcount with one reference for the rings and one for the thread, and free it with the last one. The thread can't reach a freed ring, rings leave ctx_list before dropping their reference, and the io-wq hash is refcounted.

t: io_uring: defer foreign io-wq enqueues to task_work
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring: defer foreign io-wq enqueues to task_work An IOPOLL ring without DEFER_TASKRUN can be reaped by a task other than the one that submitted the I/O. If a polled request is marked REQ_F_REISSUE, io_free_batch_list() calls io_queue_iowq() with the original tctx. Ordinary task exit can tear down tctx->io_wq after draining only the tracked requests. The live request pins the task, but not its io-wq, so the foreign task can race io_wq_put_and_exit() and enqueue through a freed or NULL queue. Forward foreign userspace enqueues to the owning task before accessing tctx->io_wq. Use a dedicated task_work callback so reissues still go straight to io-wq, and fail them if task_work is running in cancellation mode. Preserve the existing PF_KTHREAD cancellation path. This also covers the other callers of io_queue_iowq() without changing the worker-owned enqueue path.

t: io_uring/cancel: drop sqd->lock while SQPOLL waits
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring/cancel: drop sqd->lock while SQPOLL waits An exiting SQPOLL thread calls io_uring_cancel_generic() with sqd->lock held, and keeps it across cond_resched() and the sleep until nothing is in flight anymore. A zero-copy send notification can't be canceled and stays pending as long as the peer doesn't read, so the lock is held for as long as a user cares to. io_ring_exit_work() needs it to park the thread, and so do IORING_REGISTER_IOWQ_AFF and IOWQ_MAX_WORKERS. With 64 such rings sharing the thread, every iou_exit slot sleeps on the lock and no ring gets freed for anyone. Drop the lock around cond_resched() and the sleep, like the main loop of the thread does. Each walk of ctx_list is still under one hold, and nothing is kept across the unlock. The thread drops its io-wq, frees its tctx and clears sqd->thread under one hold after the loop, so whoever holds the lock and finds sqd->thread set can still use them. [axboe: adapted to the schedule_timeout() based loop]

t: io_uring/poll: cancel all matching requests in one pass
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: io_uring/poll: cancel all matching requests in one pass With IORING_ASYNC_CANCEL_ALL, __io_async_cancel() calls io_try_cancel() until nothing is found, and io_poll_cancel() cancels one request per call, starting each lookup at the beginning of the hash. A cancelled request stays hashed until its task work runs, so every lookup walks past the ones already cancelled. Cancelling K of N pending polls visits about K*N/2 requests in one io_uring_enter(), with uring_lock held. A single CANCEL_FD|ALL on 80000 polls on one eventfd takes 17.06s, 0.02s with this change. With voluntary preemption the soft lockup watchdog fires: watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#1 stuck for 26s! [repro:100] RIP: 0010:io_cancel_req_match+0x19/0xa0 io_poll_cancel+0x73/0x170 io_try_cancel+0x7b/0xf0 __io_async_cancel+0x41/0x110 Walk the hash once and cancel every match, as io_cancel_remove() does for futex and waitid. Cancel by user_data only needs its own bucket. __io_async_cancel() still loops until nothing is found, so a request that io-wq parks in the poll hash meanwhile is still cancelled. A cancel that matches one request now walks the whole hash twice instead of stopping at the match.

t: D-Link DIR-600L fatlady hedwig.cgi path traversal
d: A weakness has been identified in D-Link DIR-600L 2.17b02. Affected by this issue is some unknown functionality of the file hedwig.cgi of the component fatlady Handler. Executing a manipulation can lead to path traversal. The attack may be launched remotely.

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the web management service of the Ethernet Remote I/Os products. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient bounds checking of specially crafted HTTP requests, potentially causing the web management service to crash and resulting in a denial-of-service condition.

t: Github.com/kuadrant/kuadrant-operator: github.com/kuadrant/wasm-shim: kuadrant-operator: authpolicy is silently bypassed (fail-open) when a tokenratelimitpolicy
d: A flaw was found in the Kuadrant WebAssembly (WASM) shim shipped in Red Hat Connectivity Link 1.5. When a TokenRateLimitPolicy is attached to an HTTPRoute that also has an AuthPolicy - or when a RateLimitPolicy with defaults or overrides is attached to the Gateway or listener of such routes - the shim's action pipeline fails to dispatch the authentication guard at request time, and the request is forwarded upstream. Unauthenticated requests return 200 OK instead of 401, and neither authentication nor rate limiting is enforced. Both policies continue to report Enforced, leaving no status-level indication of the failure.

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the SNMP service of the Ethernet Remote I/Os products. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit improper handling of specially crafted SNMP requests, potentially leading to a denial-of-service condition on the affected device.

t: D-Link DIR-600L GENA gena.cgi genacgi_main os command injection
d: A vulnerability was identified in D-Link DIR-600L 2.17b02. Affected is the function genacgi_main of the file gena.cgi of the component GENA Handler. Such manipulation leads to os command injection. The attack can be launched remotely. The exploit is publicly available and might be used.

t: TRENDnet TEW-657BRM mini_httpd entries information disclosure
d: A vulnerability has been found in TRENDnet TEW-657BRM 1.00.1. The impacted element is an unknown function of the file /usr/www/images/.svn/entries of the component mini_httpd. The manipulation leads to information disclosure. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The vendor explains: "I am not able to confirm if such vulnerability exists as the product has been EOL for more than 15 years. We will send out an announcement letting customers know." This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

t: Konstanty libmodplug ABC File load_abc.cpp abc_add_drum out-of-bounds
d: A flaw has been found in Konstanty libmodplug up to 0.8.9.1. The affected element is the function abc_add_drum of the file src/load_abc.cpp of the component ABC File Handler. Executing a manipulation can lead to out-of-bounds read. The attack may be performed from remote. Upgrading to version 0.8.9.2 is sufficient to fix this issue. This patch is called 540f0b8ec3d7979e17a8d6a55e31b8a7b734d463. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component.

t: declare-lab tango Model Loading tango.py Tango.__init__ input validation
d: A vulnerability was detected in declare-lab tango up to 34ecd38898508017ca937508a047b42817d2b070. Impacted is the function Tango.__init__ of the file tango.py of the component Model Loading. Performing a manipulation of the argument scheduler_name results in improper input validation. The attack is possible to be carried out remotely. The exploit is now public and may be used. This product adopts a rolling release strategy to maintain continuous delivery. Therefore, version details for affected or updated releases cannot be specified. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

t: Lightbox with PhotoSwipe < 5.19.0 - Unauthenticated Stored XSS via Comment Link URL in Share Menu
d: The Lightbox with PhotoSwipe WordPress plugin before 5.19.0 does not escape image link URLs before outputting them in the attributes of the lightbox share menu, allowing unauthenticated users to perform Stored Cross-Site Scripting attacks via comments when the PhotoSwipe 4 frontend is used.

t: User Registration Aide <= 1.5.3.8 - Unauthenticated Account Takeover via Password Update Page
d: The User Registration Aide WordPress plugin through 1.5.3.8 does not verify the current password or a reset token before changing a user's password, allowing unauthenticated attackers who know a user's username and email address to change the password of any account, including administrators, and take it over.

An improper firmware authenticity verification vulnerability exists in the affected Ethernet Switches products. An authenticated remote attacker with administrative privileges could exploit the lack of cryptographic signature verification to install unauthorized firmware, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution on the affected device.

t: cxl/features: Ensure that count is set before access to ent[] __counted_by()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: cxl/features: Ensure that count is set before access to ent[] __counted_by() get_supported_features() assigns entries->num_features only after the memcpy() loop that fills entries->ent[] has already run. Since ent[] is __counted_by(num_features), the compiler's bounds instrumentation sees a 0-length array during that loop and FORTIFY_SOURCE trips on the memcpy. Set @num_features right after allocation, before any write into ent[], so the bound is correct for the whole lifetime of the array. This was found via a fortify panic: memcpy: detected buffer overflow: 384 byte write of buffer size 0 WARNING: lib/string_helpers.c:1035 at __fortify_report+0x54/0xa0 kernel BUG at lib/string_helpers.c:1043! Call trace: __fortify_panic+0x10/0x18 get_supported_features.isra.0+0x4a0/0x4d0 [cxl_core] devm_cxl_setup_features+0x84/0x120 [cxl_core] cxl_pci_probe+0x254/0x5e0 [cxl_pci] Same class of bug, same fix shape as commit 6c9d2e87df40 ("cxl/fwctl: Fix __fortify_panic"), which fixed the analogous issue in cxlctl_get_supported_features() but missed this one. [ dj: Fixed up title typo per Jonathan. ]

t: Bluetooth: L2CAP: Reject signalling responses in invalid states
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: Bluetooth: L2CAP: Reject signalling responses in invalid states A peer can send configuration messages while an incoming channel is in BT_CONNECT2, before the security or deferred accept gate has completed. A configuration response can then promote the channel to BT_CONNECTED. Configuration responses can also act on channels that are closing, and a late connection response can move a disconnecting channel back to BT_CONFIG. Accept connection responses only while waiting in BT_CONNECT. Answer configuration requests in BT_CONNECT2, but defer our own request until BT_CONFIG so configuration cannot complete before the gate. Ignore configuration responses outside BT_CONFIG and BT_CONNECTED, and only complete configuration in BT_CONFIG.

t: Bluetooth: L2CAP: Only accept connection responses to outstanding requests
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: Bluetooth: L2CAP: Only accept connection responses to outstanding requests An outgoing channel waits in BT_CONNECT until security and the feature mask exchange complete, and only then sends its connection request. A peer can answer it before that with a connection response matching our source CID. The channel then moves to BT_CONFIG, completes configuration and becomes connected before security has completed. If security then fails, l2cap_security_cfm() leaves the connected channel alone, so it stays up on a link that did not reach the required security level. A connection response with a zero source CID is matched by identifier. Another channel can hold the same identifier for a response it still has to send, so the lookup can pick the wrong channel. Only accept a connection response while our request is outstanding, and only look at such channels when matching by identifier.

t: smb/server: prevent file publication after tree disconnect
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb/server: prevent file publication after tree disconnect TREE_DISCONNECT closes the tree's published file handles before marking and removing the tree connection. A concurrent CREATE that already holds a tree reference can therefore publish its file after the close pass. When CREATE drops its reference, the tree can be freed while the published file still points to it. Mark and remove the tree connection before closing its files, and serialize both new-open and durable-reconnect volatile ID publication with that state transition. An opener is then either published in time for the close pass or rejected after disconnect with STATUS_NETWORK_NAME_DELETED. Keep a tree reference while a file carries its tree pointer. This protects asynchronous users that can defer the file's final destruction past tree disconnect. The close pass can race the successful FP_NEW to FP_INITED transition. Take the opening request's file reference atomically with that transition. This keeps the file alive until request completion even if teardown removes the ID immediately. BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in proc_show_files (fs/smb/server/vfs_cache.c:126) Read of size 4 at addr ff11000101540f80 by task poc/153 Call Trace: proc_show_files (fs/smb/server/vfs_cache.c:126) seq_read_iter (fs/seq_file.c:231) proc_reg_read_iter (fs/proc/inode.c:299) vfs_read (fs/read_write.c:574) ksys_read (fs/read_write.c:716) do_syscall_64 (arch/x86/entry/syscall_64.c:84) entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe (arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S:121) Allocated by: ksmbd_tree_conn_connect (fs/smb/server/mgmt/tree_connect.c:35) smb2_tree_connect (fs/smb/server/smb2pdu.c:2819) handle_ksmbd_work (fs/smb/server/server.c:368) Freed by: kfree (mm/slub.c:6801) handle_ksmbd_work (fs/smb/server/server.c:332)

t: xfs: improve dirent bounds checking in scrub and repair
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: improve dirent bounds checking in scrub and repair LOLLM complains that we don't do enough bounds checking of the directory entries in directory blocks when we're looking for errors or trying to salvage entries. Let's improve that with more detailed checks.

t: NFSD: stop registering with rpcbind after a failure in listener_set
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: NFSD: stop registering with rpcbind after a failure in listener_set nfsd_nl_listener_set_doit() calls svc_xprt_create_from_sa() once for each requested listener and passes flags of 0, so every listener registers with rpcbind on its own. A rpcbind that accepts the connection and never replies therefore costs one timeout for each entry. With the cap of 1024 entries the request can hold nfsd_mutex for about 34 minutes, which is roughly 17 times the hung-task threshold. One failure is enough to know that the next call will not fare better. Read svc_rpcb_failure_count() before the create loop, and pass SVC_SOCK_ANONYMOUS for the rest of the request once the count moves.

t: block: restore the iterator when rejecting a misaligned bio
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: block: restore the iterator when rejecting a misaligned bio bio_iov_iter_get_pages() can extract some iovecs before encountering a misaligned one. It releases the pages and rejects the entire bio, but leaves the supplied iterator advanced. An iomap direct-I/O caller may subsequently reexpand the iterator's byte count and fall back to buffered I/O. The reexpanded count then includes bytes before the iterator's current segment, potentially causing iterate_iovec() to read beyond the imported iovec array. In a reproducer using an initial empty iovec followed by 10-byte and 1015-byte segments, writev() returned 1015 instead of 1025 and KASAN reported an 8-byte read beyond the nine-element iovec allocation. Saving and restoring the iterator on the rejected-bio path makes writev() return 1025 and eliminates the KASAN report. Restore the entire iterator rather than reverting a byte count: advancing past an empty segment changes its position without consuming any bytes. Leave successful and partially accepted bio paths unchanged.

t: ACPI: CPPC: Validate FFH register fields before hardware access
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ACPI: CPPC: Validate FFH register fields before hardware access The x86 CPPC FFH accessors construct masks and shift values using the firmware's Bit Width and Bit Offset without checking that the field fits in an MSR. A zero-width field or a field extending beyond bit 63 can therefore cause an invalid shift. The safe MSR accessors only handle an access fault, not invalid field arithmetic after a successful read. Also, the 64-bit GAS address is implicitly narrowed to the 32-bit MSR number. A descriptor with nonzero upper address bits can access a different MSR from the one described by firmware. The arm64 AMU counter readers have the same unchecked field arithmetic. Validate the field bounds before reading a counter, including both descriptors in the paired counter path. Dispatch FFH accesses before decoding the GAS Access Size in the common read and write paths. Otherwise, a large access_width can trigger an invalid shift in GET_BIT_WIDTH() before the architecture validates its register. That field has architecture-specific FFH semantics and is not needed by the generic memory/port accessor on this path. Validate x86 MSR addresses and share the field-bounds checks between related accessors within each architecture.

t: cpufreq: CPPC: Select the frequency-invariance callback per CPU
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: cpufreq: CPPC: Select the frequency-invariance callback per CPU cppc_cpufreq_cpu_fie_init() initializes deferred work only for CPUs whose feedback counters use PCC. However, if any CPU in a shared policy uses PCC, it installs the PCC tick callback for the entire policy. With FIE enabled, a non-PCC CPU then queues an uninitialized irq_work and can call a NULL function pointer when that work runs. Choose the frequency-invariance callback separately for each CPU using the recorded work-initialization state. Processor removal can unpublish the CPC descriptor before callback registration, so querying its counter transport again can incorrectly select direct reads for a PCC CPU. Register the callbacks after all counter initialization has completed, so a failed initial read for an online CPU cannot leave a partially registered policy. PCC CPUs use their initialized deferred work, while non-PCC CPUs read their own counters directly from the tick.

t: xfrm: retry inexact policy lookup after node reinsertion
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfrm: retry inexact policy lookup after node reinsertion An inexact policy lookup first records pointers to candidate hlist heads and then traverses the lists. A concurrent policy insertion can merge inexact tree nodes between those operations: lookup policy insertion ------ ---------------- find inexact candidates save obsolete hlist head write_seqcount_begin(&bin->count) merge inexact tree nodes hlist_del_rcu(&policy->bydst) reinsert policy->bydst in survivor write_seqcount_end(&bin->count) evaluate saved candidate list miss the moved policy The merge immediately reinserts the same hlist node into the surviving tree node. RCU keeps the policy alive, but it does not provide a consistent view while its list node is moved. A lookup that selected the obsolete list can observe it empty. A lookup already traversing a moved policy can instead follow the next pointer rewritten by the reinsertion. Either case can return an incorrect IPsec policy result. The per-bin sequence counter already brackets calls to xfrm_policy_inexact_insert_node(), including node merges. The read side, however, currently validates the counter only while searching an individual rb-tree. A successful search returns without validation, and the later candidate-list traversal is outside that read-side section. Snapshot the per-bin sequence before discovering candidate heads and validate it after evaluating all candidate lists. Retry the lookup if the inexact policy tree changes while it is being searched.

t: 9p/trans_virtio: reject mount tags longer than NAME_MAX at probe
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: 9p/trans_virtio: reject mount tags longer than NAME_MAX at probe p9_virtio_probe() reads a 16-bit mount tag length (tag_len) from the device config and kzalloc()s tag_len + 1 bytes for chan->tag with no upper bound. A malicious or compromised host can present a tag of up to 65535 bytes; that tag is later copied into the single-page sysfs buffer by p9_mount_tag_show() (memcpy(buf, chan->tag, tag_len + 1)), a host-controlled out-of-bounds write of up to ~64 KiB past the PAGE_SIZE attribute buffer. Reject an overlong tag at probe time. A 9p mount tag is a name-like identifier, so bound it by NAME_MAX (255): that limit is independent of the sysfs/seq_file page size and is far above any legitimate mount tag, which keeps p9_mount_tag_show() safe at the root without hard-coding a seq_file implementation detail.

t: 9p/xen: fix refcount leak in p9_xen_response() on wrong tag
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: 9p/xen: fix refcount leak in p9_xen_response() on wrong tag p9_xen_response() looks up the request for an incoming reply with p9_tag_lookup(), which takes a reference on the returned p9_req_t. When the tag does not resolve to a request in REQ_STATUS_SENT, the function warns and continues the loop without dropping that reference, permanently leaking the p9_req_t and its msize buffers. The reply header, including the tag, is supplied by the backend, so a malicious or buggy 9P backend can leak kernel memory on every crafted response. Drop the reference before continuing.

t: net/9p/usbg: Fix use-after-free in disable_usb9pfs()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/9p/usbg: Fix use-after-free in disable_usb9pfs() disable_usb9pfs() frees the IN and OUT usb_request objects before it disables the corresponding endpoints. If either request is still queued, the later usb_ep_disable() call cancels the endpoint queue and the UDC driver can still access the already freed request. With dummy_hcd and KASAN, this is reproducible by queueing the OUT request and then disconnecting the configfs gadget: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in dummy_disable+0x2b4/0x300 Read of size 8 at addr ffff888009702400 by task sh/1 usb_ep_disable+0x8e/0x1f0 usb9pfs_func_unbind+0x193/0x350 gadget_dev_desc_UDC_store+0x135/0x280 dummy_free_request() also warns because the request is freed while its queue entry is still linked. Disable both endpoints before freeing the request objects. This lets usb_ep_disable() cancel any queued transfers and invoke the completion callback while the request storage is still valid. The request objects are then freed only after they have been removed from the endpoint queues.

t: net/9p/usbg: also disable endpoints on p9_usbg_close
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/9p/usbg: also disable endpoints on p9_usbg_close The close function has to fully reverse the state change of 9p_create (mount) and the potential call of set_alt(1). This includes to ensure that the usage of the endpoints is not active any more.

t: net/9p/usbg: set client to Disconnected on usb9pfs_disable
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/9p/usbg: set client to Disconnected on usb9pfs_disable This patch is setting the client status to Disconnected, when the client is still in use. Otherwise a disconnected usb cable would run any use of the mount to faults.

t: net/9p/usbg: always reset completion when disconnecting
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/9p/usbg: always reset completion when disconnecting When some tx or rx transfers were pending while closing the connection, the completion handler could catch one pending completion call. To ensure a normal start when mounting again, we have to reset the completion and flush any pending completions.

t: net/9p/usbg: call disable_usb9pfs() from usb9pfs_disable()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/9p/usbg: call disable_usb9pfs() from usb9pfs_disable() usb9pfs_disable() is the usb_function ->disable callback, invoked by the composite gadget core whenever the host resets or unconfigures the gadget. The gadget function API requires this callback to disable its endpoints; every other in-tree function driver does so from its ->disable hook. usb9pfs_disable() never called disable_usb9pfs(), so the IN/OUT endpoints and their usb_request objects were left active and allocated across a host-driven disable. When the host later reconfigures the device, enable_usb9pfs() calls alloc_requests() again and unconditionally overwrites usb9pfs->in_req/out_req, permanently leaking the previous allocations, while the endpoints themselves are left enabled underneath the function's own idea of being disabled. Call disable_usb9pfs() before reinit_completion(&usb9pfs->send), mirroring the same sequence already used in p9_usbg_close(). Placing it before the reinit_completion() also ensures usb_ep_disable() has synchronously flushed any requests still queued in hardware before the completion is reset, closing the same race that motivated resetting the completion here in the first place.

t: net/9p/usbg: fix out_req buffer leak in disable_usb9pfs
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/9p/usbg: fix out_req buffer leak in disable_usb9pfs usb9pfs->out_req is allocated with alloc_ep_req(), which also allocates the request's data buffer (req->buf). disable_usb9pfs() frees it with plain usb_ep_free_request(), which only frees the usb_request structure itself and leaks req->buf on every close. Use free_ep_req() instead, matching the allocator, as documented by its own comment ("Requests allocated via alloc_ep_req() *must* be freed by free_ep_req()").

t: net/9p/usbg: remove bogus context initialization in alloc_requests
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/9p/usbg: remove bogus context initialization in alloc_requests alloc_requests() initializes usb9pfs->in_req->context to point at the struct f_usb9pfs instance itself. usb9pfs_queue_tx() later overwrites this with the real struct p9_req_t pointer before every transmit, and usb9pfs_tx_complete() clears it back to NULL after each completion, so in_req->context only ever holds a valid p9_req_t once a request has actually been queued. usb9pfs_clear_tx(), however, can run at any time (mount close, gadget disable) independent of whether a request was ever queued. If it runs before the first usb9pfs_transmit(), it reads the leftover sentinel value, type-confuses the struct f_usb9pfs pointer as a struct p9_req_t, and both writes through it (req->t_err = -ECONNRESET) and hands it to p9_client_cb(), which manipulates req->wq and req->refcount at bogus offsets inside f_usb9pfs. This reliably corrupts memory or panics whenever the transport is torn down before any 9p request has been transmitted, e.g. mounting and immediately unmounting, or a cable disconnect racing the very first request. usb9pfs->out_req->context is set the same way but is never read by this transport (usb9pfs_rx_complete() identifies the instance via ep->driver_data instead), so it serves no purpose either. Both endpoints' ->driver_data are already set to usb9pfs in enable_endpoint(), which is what the completion handlers actually use to recover the f_usb9pfs instance. Just drop the leftover ->context assignments; usb_ep_alloc_request()/alloc_ep_req() already return zeroed requests, so in_req->context correctly starts out NULL.

t: net/9p/usbg: clear stale client pointer on close
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/9p/usbg: clear stale client pointer on close p9_usbg_close() tears down the client transport, but usb9pfs keeps using usb9pfs->client from asynchronous TX and RX completion handlers. A late completion can therefore dereference a client that has already been freed during mount teardown. Clear usb9pfs->client under usb9pfs->lock when closing the transport, detach any pending TX request from in_req->context, and make the TX/RX completion handlers bail out once the transport has been detached. This keeps late completions from touching a freed or rebound p9_client.

t: xfrm: interface: validate the IP header on xmit
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfrm: interface: validate the IP header on xmit Packets injected into an xfrm interface (e.g. AF_PACKET on an xfrmi device) reach the xfrm output path without IP header validation, but xfrm4_transport_output() uses iph->ihl for __skb_pull() and memmove() and expects the header to be valid. vti_tunnel_xmit() already calls pskb_inet_may_pull() before handing packets to the xfrm output path. Do the same in xfrmi_xmit() and perform the header checks ip_rcv_core()/ip6_rcv_core() do on entry to the IP stack: reject wrong IP versions and malformed IPv4 header lengths.

t: xfrm: espintcp: reorder operations within espintcp_init_sk
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfrm: espintcp: reorder operations within espintcp_init_sk When enabled on a socket, espintcp sets the socket callbacks to its own before it has finished setting up its context and published it as icsk_ulp_data. Any one of those callbacks that gets called before will dereference a NULL icsk_ulp_data. Fix this by reording the operations, and add memory barriers to ensure callers will have a struct espintcp_ctx available. Add a few WRITE_ONCE/READ_ONCE too while we're there.

t: drm/drm_crtc: ensure dma_fence_ops remain valid during device unbind
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/drm_crtc: ensure dma_fence_ops remain valid during device unbind In [1], sashiko reported the following issue: === snip === Looking at how these fences are managed, drm_crtc_create_fence() creates a dma_fence without taking a reference to the drm_device or drm_crtc. Because the sync_file framework exposes this fence to userspace, the fence can outlive the CRTC. The dma_fence contract requires that data accessed by dma_fence_ops (like get_driver_name) must remain valid for an RCU grace period after the fence is signaled. However, drm_crtc_cleanup() and the subsequent freeing of the device do not wait for an RCU grace period via synchronize_rcu(). If userspace calls ioctl(SYNC_IOC_FILE_INFO) concurrently with a device hot-unplug: CPU1 (Userspace) sync_file_get_name() ops = rcu_dereference(fence->ops); if (!dma_fence_test_signaled_flag()) // Preempted or delayed here CPU2 (Driver Teardown) Signals the fence (setting fence->ops = NULL) Destroys and frees the CRTC without waiting for an RCU grace period CPU1 (Resumes) ops->get_driver_name(fence) -> drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name() crtc = fence_to_crtc(fence); // Casts to the freed CRTC return crtc->dev->driver->name; // Use-after-free ... Does the CRTC or DRM device need to be kept alive for the RCU grace period, or should the fence hold a proper reference to prevent the use-after-free when get_driver_name() and get_timeline_name() access the freed CRTC structure? === snap === I believe this to be a correct observation and this patch implements the suggestion of waiting for an RCU grace period before proceeding with destruction of the drm_crtc, so that get_driver_name() and get_timeline_name() can still work.

t: drm/drm_crtc: fix race with dma_fence_signal() in ::get_driver_name()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/drm_crtc: fix race with dma_fence_signal() in ::get_driver_name() Since commit 541c8f2468b9 ("dma-buf: detach fence ops on signal v3"), I'm seeing the BUG_ON() triggering in drm_crtc's fence_to_crtc() via drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name() regularly: Call trace: panic+0x58/0x5c die+0x160/0x178 bug_brk_handler+0x70/0xa4 call_el1_break_hook+0x3c/0x1a0 do_el1_brk64+0x24/0x74 el1_brk64+0x34/0x54 el1h_64_sync_handler+0x80/0xfc el1h_64_sync+0x84/0x88 drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name+0x60/0x68 (P) sync_file_get_name+0x184/0x45c sync_file_ioctl+0x404/0xf70 __arm64_sys_ioctl+0x124/0x1dc This looks to be caused by a code flow similar to the following: +++ snip +++ thread A thread B ioctl(SYNC_IOC_FILE_INFO) sync_file_ioctl() sync_file_get_name() dma_fence_signal_timestamp_locked() dma_fence_driver_name() ops = rcu_dereference(fence->ops) if (!dma_fence_test_signaled_flag()) ops->get_driver_name(fence) i.e. drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name() test_and_set_bit(SIGNALED) RCU_INIT_POINTER(fence->ops, NULL) drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name() BUG_ON(rcu_access_pointer(fence->ops) != &drm_crtc_fence_ops) +++ snap +++ In other words, a fence's ops pointer can now change to NULL on signal, which wasn't the case before the culprit commit and hence the BUG_ON() triggers. Simply drop the BUG_ON() as it's usage of fence ops is invalid now, and because using BUG_ON() and friends to take down the system is an unacceptable way to handle a failure. Note that the adjacent drm_crtc_fence_get_timeline_name() has the same problem and is fixed by this patch as well.

t: wifi: mac80211: reload TDLS header pointer after skb_linearize()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: mac80211: reload TDLS header pointer after skb_linearize() ieee80211_process_tdls_channel_switch() sets tf = skb->data before it calls skb_linearize(), and reads tf->action_code afterwards. ieee80211_rx_h_data() queues TDLS channel switch requests and responses to the interface after pulling only offsetof(struct ieee80211_tdls_data, u) bytes, so the skb can still be non-linear when the interface work handles it. Drivers that build paged RX skbs do this for every frame that does not fit into the skb head, e.g. iwlwifi (mvm), which is also the only mac80211 driver that sets NL80211_FEATURE_TDLS_CHANNEL_SWITCH. If the remaining data does not fit into the tailroom, skb_linearize() moves the data to a new head and frees the old one, and the action code is then read from freed memory. Depending on what that memory holds by then, the frame is handled as before or ends in the WARN_ON_ONCE() of the default case. The frame only has to be a data frame with the TDLS ethertype from an authorized peer, e.g. relayed by the AP from another station in the BSS; the read happens before the sender is checked to be a TDLS peer. Load tf after skb_linearize(), as the request and response handlers already do. Found by static analysis tool CodeQL.

t: drm/vc4: Publish the output fence outside of job_lock
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/vc4: Publish the output fence outside of job_lock job_lock is taken by the V3D interrupt handler, so nesting an IRQ-unsafe lock under it creates an inversion. drm_syncobj_replace_fence() takes drm_syncobj::lock, which other paths acquire with interrupts enabled. For example, a thread interrupted while holding it blocks the handler on job_lock, and the handler can only make progress once the submit path releases job_lock, which it cannot do while waiting for drm_syncobj::lock. This is reported by lockdep: [ 188.139076] ======================================================== [ 188.139086] WARNING: possible irq lock inversion dependency detected [ 188.139096] 7.3.0-rc3-00067-gc4f3feeaf60f #67 Tainted: G C [ 188.139108] -------------------------------------------------------- [ 188.139116] swapper/0/0 just changed the state of lock: [ 188.139125] ffff0000054f8ff8 (&vc4->job_lock){-...}-{3:3}, at: vc4_irq+0xa8/0x28c [vc4] [ 188.139234] but this lock took another, HARDIRQ-unsafe lock in the past: [ 188.139242] (&syncobj->lock){+.+.}-{3:3} [ 188.139256] and interrupts could create inverse lock ordering between them. [ 188.139267] other info that might help us debug this: [ 188.139275] Possible interrupt unsafe locking scenario: [ 188.139284] CPU0 CPU1 [ 188.139291] ---- ---- [ 188.139299] lock(&syncobj->lock); [ 188.139312] local_irq_disable(); [ 188.139320] lock(&vc4->job_lock); [ 188.139335] lock(&syncobj->lock); [ 188.139350] <Interrupt> [ 188.139358] lock(&vc4->job_lock); [ 188.139372] *** DEADLOCK *** Hand the fence over after job_lock is dropped. The job can complete and drop exec->fence in that window, so take a reference first and publish through the local pointer, as exec may already be gone.

t: drm/vc4: Drop the BO reservations outside of job_lock
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/vc4: Drop the BO reservations outside of job_lock vc4_queue_submit() calls drm_exec_fini() with job_lock held and interrupts disabled. Besides unlocking the reservations, drm_exec_fini() frees the object array with kvfree(), which asks for preemptible task context or a non-NMI interrupt, and may reach might_sleep() through vfree(). Considering that an array that exceeds a page can take the vmalloc fallback, call drm_exec_fini() once job_lock is dropped. The reservations are then held across the job kick, which is harmless as nothing in the completion path takes a BO reservation. Note that vc4_attach_fences() has to stay inside the critical section, as it walks exec, which the job done worker is free to release as soon as job_lock is dropped.

t: wifi: mac80211: reinstate IEEE80211_TX_CTL_AMPDU flag in ieee80211_tx_prep_agg()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: mac80211: reinstate IEEE80211_TX_CTL_AMPDU flag in ieee80211_tx_prep_agg() The commit 592234e941f1 ("wifi: mac80211: Fix iTXQ AMPDU fragmentation handling") changed the way handling of the IEEE80211_TX_CTL_AMPDU flag is done in mac80211, so the only place it is set is in ieee80211_tx_dequeue(). This means that any frames that are sent to the driver via drv_tx() will no longer have the flag set. In particular, this affects packets going through ieee80211_tx_pending(). Evan reported that this can result in the ath9k driver failing to account such packets in its block ack window, eventually overrunning the window and stalling TX. Fix this by reinstating the flag in ieee80211_tx_prep_agg() when inside a valid block ack window. This should be harmless for the TXQ path, and will reinstate the previous behaviour for drivers that use the flag as a signal to track the packet in the window.

t: xfrm4: use a full socket for local errors
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfrm4: use a full socket for local errors xfrm4_local_error() passes skb->sk to inet_sk() and ip_local_error() without ensuring it points to a full socket. TCP SYN-ACK skbs can be owned by TCP_NEW_SYN_RECV request sockets. xfrm4_tunnel_check_size() already checks sk_fullsock() since commit 1620c88887b1 ("xfrm: Fix the usage of skb->sk"), so iptfs_is_too_big() is the only remaining IPv4 caller passing a request socket here: the sk it tests is the listener, while skb->sk is the request socket. When IP-TFS rejects such an skb because it exceeds its payload MTU, the local error path treats the request socket as a struct inet_sock. KASAN reports a slab-out-of-bounds read in ip_local_error() beyond the request_sock_TCP allocation. Resolve the skb owner with skb_to_full_sk() before accessing inet_sock state or reporting the error. This maps a request socket to its listener and rejects sockets that cannot be used as full sockets, matching what commit 6973a21ee73c ("ipv6: xfrm: use full sockets in local error paths") did for xfrm6_local_error().

t: scsi: aic79xx: Fix NULL pointer dereference in device reset
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: scsi: aic79xx: Fix NULL pointer dereference in device reset Since commit c67e63800446 ("scsi: aic79xx: Do not reference SCSI command when resetting device") the device reset SCB has no SCSI command, but ahd_linux_dev_reset() still sets its residual, and ahd_abort_scbs(), which completes it, sets its status. Seen on an AIC-7902 when a failing disk triggered a device reset, which killed the SCSI error handler: BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000009c EIP: ahd_linux_dev_reset.cold+0xee/0x26e Add NULL command checks to the accessors in aic79xx_osm.h. Also skip autosense for an SCB without a command and complete it with ahd_done() right away: the REQUEST SENSE path can clear SCB_DEVICE_RESET, after which ahd_done() would dereference the missing command.

t: scsi: target: Fix demo-mode dynamic ACL dev-entry UAF vs LUN teardown
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: scsi: target: Fix demo-mode dynamic ACL dev-entry UAF vs LUN teardown A demo-mode (generate_node_acls=1) login that allocates a dynamic NodeACL populates that ACL's per-LUN dev entries in core_tpg_add_node_to_devs() *before* the ACL is linked onto tpg->acl_node_list by target_add_node_acl(): core_tpg_check_initiator_node_acl(): ... core_tpg_add_node_to_devs(acl, tpg, NULL); /* builds deves */ target_add_node_acl(acl); /* only now listed */ The LUN teardown sweep, core_clear_lun_from_tpg(), enumerates only tpg->acl_node_list, so a dev entry whose ACL is still in the window above is invisible to the sweep and is never disabled. It is left on the se_lun->lun_deve_list after core_tpg_remove_lun() frees the se_lun; when the same unpacked_lun is later re-added and the se_lun is reallocated at the same address, the stale dev entry is rediscovered by target_nacl_find_deve() and core_enable_device_list_for_node() corrupts lun_deve_list: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free ... core_enable_device_list_for_node+0x5ce/0x880 core_tpg_add_node_to_devs+0x169/0x190 core_dev_add_lun+0x146/0x190 target_fabric_port_link+0xe9/0x1b0 configfs_symlink+0x381/0xae0 __x64_sys_symlink+0x55/0x80 The demo-mode login path that drives the ACL/dev-entry creation is reachable by an unauthenticated initiator; the colliding LUN add/remove is a local configfs operation. Commit 49cb77e297dc ("target: Avoid mappedlun symlink creation during lun shutdown") introduced se_lun->lun_shutdown and guarded the *explicit* ACL MappedLUN path (target_fabric_mappedlun_link()), but the demo-mode automatic path, core_tpg_add_node_to_devs() -> core_enable_device_list_for_node(), was never given the equivalent guard, and the publish-after-populate ordering in core_tpg_check_initiator_node_acl() was left unchanged. Fix it in three cooperating parts: 1) Publish the dynamic NodeACL onto acl_node_list *before* creating its dev entries, so the teardown sweep can observe them. 2) Refuse to attach a dev entry to an se_lun that is shutting down, checked under nacl->lun_entry_mutex -- the same lock the sweep takes -- so once the sweep has passed an ACL any later enable for that LUN observes lun_shutdown and skips it. 3) In core_enable_device_list_for_node(), insert the new dev entry onto lun->lun_deve_list while still holding nacl->lun_entry_mutex, in both the replace and the new-entry branch. Previously the entry was added to nacl->lun_entry_hlist under the mutex but to lun->lun_deve_list only after dropping it; with the ACL now published early, the sweep could take the mutex in that gap, find the entry on the hlist, core_disable_device_list_for_node() it (list_del() on the not-yet- linked lun_link succeeds and the entry is freed), and then the enable would list_add_tail() the freed entry back onto lun_deve_list. Linking both lists under the mutex makes enable and the sweep mutually exclusive, closing that window. core_tpg_add_node_to_devs() already ignores the return value of core_enable_device_list_for_node(), so a shutting-down LUN is simply skipped.

t: 9p/xen: validate the response size from the backend
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: 9p/xen: validate the response size from the backend p9_xen_response() takes the length of an incoming response from the ring -- the first field of the 9p header, which the Xen transport reuses as its framing header -- and uses it to advance the consumer index, but never checks that it is at least the header size or no larger than the number of bytes the backend has actually produced. A malicious or buggy backend can post a response whose size is smaller than the header (for example 0). The consumer index then never advances, so the response work re-reads the same ring contents instead of making progress. In testing this raced with the teardown that the malformed reply triggers and dereferenced a freed p9_client: 9pfs 9pfs-0: Wrong req tag=ffff BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000060 #PF: supervisor read access in kernel mode #PF: error_code(0x0000) - not-present page PGD 0 P4D 0 Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP NOPTI CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 11 Comm: kworker/0:1 Not tainted 7.2.0-rc5 #6 PREEMPT(lazy) Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (Q35 + ICH9, 2009), BIOS rel-1.17.0-0-gb52ca86e094d-prebuilt.qemu.org 04/01/2014 Workqueue: events p9_xen_response RIP: 0010:idr_find+0x4/0x10 RSP: 0018:ffffbf5d80063de8 EFLAGS: 00010202 RAX: 0000000000000001 RBX: ffffa229c21195a0 RCX: ffffa229c2400000 RDX: ffffa229c11c2200 RSI: 000000000000ffff RDI: 0000000000000050 RBP: 000000000000ffff R08: 3fffffffffffdfff R09: ffffffffffffffff R10: 3fffffffffffdfff R11: ffffffff87a60e80 R12: 0000000000000050 R13: 0000000000000000 R14: 000000000000ffff R15: 0000000000100000 FS: 0000000000000000(0000) GS:ffffa22a7661c000(0000) knlGS:0000000000000000 CS: 0010 DS: 0000 ES: 0000 CR0: 0000000080050033 CR2: 0000000000000060 CR3: 000000003ac34002 CR4: 0000000000770ef0 PKRU: 55555554 Call Trace: <TASK> p9_tag_lookup+0x2b/0x90 p9_xen_response+0x17c/0x2e0 process_one_work+0x16a/0x3a0 worker_thread+0x172/0x2e0 kthread+0xdd/0x110 ret_from_fork+0x18b/0x240 ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30 </TASK> Modules linked in: CR2: 0000000000000060 ---[ end trace 0000000000000000 ]--- Reject a response whose size is outside [sizeof(header), queued] before using it, matching the validation the backend already applies to incoming requests.

t: 9p: don't decrement a server-owned zero nlink
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: 9p: don't decrement a server-owned zero nlink A 9P2000.L server can report nlink=0 for a regular file that still exists. On a cache=loose or cache=fscache mount, lookup stores that value with set_nlink(). A later successful unlink calls v9fs_dec_count(), which still calls drop_nlink() for a non-directory. drop_nlink() warns, and the unsigned link count wraps to 4294967295. fstat() on a descriptor opened before the unlink shows 0 before and 4294967295 after. The warning on the unpatched kernel, trimmed: WARNING: fs/inode.c:408 at drop_nlink+0xac/0xd0, CPU#1: trigger/188 CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 188 Comm: trigger Tainted: G N 7.3.0-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820 #1 PREEMPT(lazy) RIP: 0010:drop_nlink+0xac/0xd0 Call Trace: <TASK> v9fs_remove+0x529/0x750 vfs_unlink+0x2f0/0xbd0 filename_unlinkat+0x340/0x6c0 __x64_sys_unlink+0x46/0x70 do_syscall_64+0xe8/0x4f0 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f </TASK> ---[ end trace 0000000000000000 ]--- Directories whose cached nlink is at most 2 already skip this decrement, because the exported filesystem may not maintain nlink (commit ac89b2ef9b559). cache=none skips it as well (commit 574aa0b479947). cache=mmap does not take this path: it sets neither CACHE_META nor CACHE_LOOSE. A regular file on cache=loose or cache=fscache still does. Its count came from GETATTR and may already be zero, so skip the decrement when i_nlink is already 0. Verified on 7.3-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820 with only this change. A server that advertises nlink=0 and accepts the unlink no longer warns, and the open descriptor stays at nlink 0. An honest server on the same mount still goes from 1 to 0. A rejected unlink leaves the count unchanged. cache=none is unchanged. With panic_on_warn the unpatched kernel panics on the warning; the patched kernel does not.

t: batman-adv: mcast: validate tracker padding before forwarding
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: mcast: validate tracker padding before forwarding A multicast tracker with an even number of destinations needs two padding bytes after its destination list. batadv_mcast_forw_packet() currently only checks that the count field and the addresses fit in the tracker TVLV. If an unpadded even tracker is compacted to an odd number of destinations, batadv_mcast_forw_shrink_update_headers() includes those missing padding bytes in the amount to remove. The subsequent memmove can then write two bytes past the old packet tail. With no tailroom, this corrupts skb_shared_info. Include the required padding in the existing tracker length check. This rejects the malformed tracker before either received or locally generated packets can reach the compactor.

t: batman-adv: stop originator purge worker before freeing TT
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: stop originator purge worker before freeing TT batadv_mesh_free() releases the translation tables via batadv_tt_free() before batadv_originator_free() stops orig_work. The purge worker can therefore still run while the TT is torn down. When an originator times out, batadv_purge_orig_ref() calls batadv_tt_global_del_orig(), which loads tt.global_hash and walks all buckets while taking their locks: CPU0 CPU1 batadv_tt_free() batadv_purge_orig() batadv_tt_global_del_orig() hash = ...tt.global_hash; batadv_tt_global_table_free() batadv_hash_destroy(hash); spin_lock_bh(&hash->list_locks[i]); Disable orig_work at the beginning of batadv_mesh_free(), directly after the mesh was marked as deactivating. The second disable_delayed_work_sync() in batadv_originator_free() is harmless because it is free'd anyway.

t: batman-adv: tt: ignore ROAM flag of received ADD changes
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: tt: ignore ROAM flag of received ADD changes A received TT change (OGM diff or full table response) with the ROAM flag but without DEL is handled by batadv_tt_global_add() like a ROAMING_ADV: * a newly created global entry gets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM and is therefore excluded from the global CRC. The sender has it in its local CRC and the receiver has to request the full table again * batadv_tt_global_purge_local() removes the local entry of the receiver. The receiver's own client is considered as roamed to the sender and frames for it are rerouted The ROAM flag only has a meaning together with DEL. Drop it on reception to keep it from populating the global table with a temporary ROAMING entry which is not part of the CRC - and therefore causing a CRC mismatch.

t: batman-adv: tt: don't drop local events queued during TVLV update
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: tt: don't drop local events queued during TVLV update batadv_tt_tvlv_container_update() read the number of local changes without holding changes_list_lock. batadv_tt_local_event() is not serialized by the commit_lock and can queue new events before the changes_list is flushed: CPU0 CPU1 batadv_tt_tvlv_container_update() num = ...local_changes; batadv_tt_local_event() list_add_tail(...); ...local_changes++; spin_lock_bh(&...changes_list_lock); /* only num events copied but all freed */ The additional events were freed without ever being sent. Other nodes will only notice this via a CRC mismatch and must request the full table. The number of changes and the changes_list must therefore be taken atomically. Events queued afterwards then stay in the tt.changes_list for the next TT round. The changes can no longer be kept for the next round when the TVLV buffer allocation fails. But they would be sent with a skipped TTVN anyway, so the other nodes have to request the full table in this case either way. The last changeset is only dropped in this case when the TTVN was incremented. Without new changes, it still describes the current TTVN. Previously, the unconsumed changes caused a retry of the TVLV container update in the next commit round. Since the changes are now consumed, the next round would only take the path without changes and wait for BATADV_TT_OGM_APPEND_MAX rounds before updating the container again. Until then, the outdated container with the previous TTVN would still be announced. The ogm_append_cnt is therefore reset on failure to retry the update in the next OGM interval. This doesn't make the CRC consistent with the announced changeset. The local table modifications are still not serialized with the commit and batadv_tt_local_transition_new() can still make a client part of the CRC for which the event is only part of the next TT round. Such an inconsistency is detected by the CRC check of the other nodes and solved via a full table request.

t: sctp: account for chunk padding in sctp_init_cause()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sctp: account for chunk padding in sctp_init_cause() sctp_init_cause() accepts a chunk when skb_tailroom() can hold the cause header and the payload. sctp_addto_chunk() then writes 0-3 bytes of padding before that header so the chunk stays 4-byte aligned. The check does not include the padding, and the following skb_put() calls skb_over_panic() from softirq. Count the padding sctp_addto_chunk() is about to write. The cause length on the wire stays the header plus the payload. Found by LLM inspection, triggered and tested the fix.

t: btrfs: sysfs: restore NOFS context on early return in btrfs_sysfs_add_block_group_type()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: btrfs: sysfs: restore NOFS context on early return in btrfs_sysfs_add_block_group_type() btrfs_sysfs_add_block_group_type() sets up a NOFS context with memalloc_nofs_save() because kobject_add() performs GFP_KERNEL allocations deep in its call chain, and the function may be called while holding a transaction handle or a lock required for a transaction commit, where reclaim could deadlock. Every other return path of this function calls memalloc_nofs_restore() except the early return taken when another thread has already created the kobject for the same raid index (this can happen when restriping). Taking that path leaves PF_MEMALLOC_NOFS set on the calling task, so all subsequent memory allocations performed by that task remain restricted to the NOFS scope, which may lead to unexpected allocation failures or deadlocks later on. Restore the NOFS context before returning from that path.

t: btrfs: prevent deleting the wrong subvolume by ID
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: btrfs: prevent deleting the wrong subvolume by ID When deleting a subvolume by ID, btrfs_ioctl_snap_destroy() first resolves the requested ID to a name, then looks up that name again under the parent directory lock. A concurrent rename can change which subvolume is associated with the name between these operations. Since the deletion path does not verify the ID of the resolved subvolume, it can delete a different subvolume while leaving the requested one intact. This was reproduced by repeatedly exchanging the names of two subvolumes using renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE) while deleting one of them by ID. The wrong subvolume was deleted in 9 out of 14 independent tests. Fix this by checking that the resolved subvolume ID matches the requested ID while holding the parent directory lock. Return -EAGAIN on a mismatch so that userspace can retry the operation instead of being told that the requested subvolume does not exist.

A hard-coded cryptographic key vulnerability exists in affected Ethernet swiches. The use of a shared cryptographic key with insufficient key strength could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker, under certain conditions, to impersonate affected devices and potentially compromise the confidentiality and integrity of communications.

t: ptp: fix use-after-free in extts_fifo_show() reading tsevqs unlocked
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ptp: fix use-after-free in extts_fifo_show() reading tsevqs unlocked extts_fifo_show() walks ptp->tsevqs with list_count_nodes() and then list_first_entry() without holding ptp->tsevqs_lock, the spinlock that "protects tsevqs from concurrent access". Every other accessor of the list honours it: ptp_open() (list_add_tail), ptp_release() (list_del followed by kfree of the per-fd queue), ptp_clock_release() and ptp_clock_event() all take tsevqs_lock. extts_fifo_show() is the only one that does not. A per-fd timestamp queue is appended to tsevqs on open("/dev/ptpN") and removed and freed on close(), both under tsevqs_lock: scoped_guard(spinlock_irq, &ptp->tsevqs_lock) list_del(&queue->qlist); bitmap_free(queue->mask); kfree(queue); So a read of /sys/class/ptp/ptpN/fifo running concurrently with a close() of a /dev/ptpN fd can have list_count_nodes() walk into the queue that close() is removing and freeing, dereferencing freed memory (use-after-free) or a poisoned list pointer. Take tsevqs_lock around the list walk. The fifo only ever draws from the first queue, which is the registration-time queue created in ptp_clock_register() and freed only in ptp_clock_release(); that cannot run while the sysfs attribute is being read, so the dequeue from queue->buf under queue->lock may stay outside tsevqs_lock and the lock order is unchanged.

t: scsi: target: Verify the iSCSI ISID is null-terminated
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: scsi: target: Verify the iSCSI ISID is null-terminated iscsi_parse_pr_out_transport_id() returns the ISID of a FORMAT CODE 01b TransportID as a pointer into the PERSISTENT RESERVE OUT parameter list, lowercased in place and never null-terminated. spc4r37 Table 508 requires the field to be null-terminated, but a non-conforming initiator can omit the NULL; when the ISID ends at the end of the received buffer, the pointer is not a C string. The registration code still consumes it as one: strcmp() in __core_scsi3_locate_pr_reg() and in the REGISTER AND MOVE path, and snprintf("%s") in __core_scsi3_do_alloc_registration(), which also reads its first 8 bytes unconditionally with get_unaligned_be64() - a NUL check does not bound that read. When the parameter list spans more than one page, transport_kmap_data_sg() maps it with vmap(), and the over-read walks off the end of the mapping into the vmalloc() guard page and oopses. Reproduced with a PR OUT REGISTER + SPEC_I_PT parameter list of exactly 8192 bytes whose final TransportID carries a 12-byte ISID without a terminating NUL: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffc9000138c000 RIP: 0010:strcmp+0xc/0x30 Call Trace: __core_scsi3_locate_pr_reg+0xd3/0x120 [target_core_mod] core_scsi3_decode_spec_i_port+0x8fc/0x13a0 [target_core_mod] core_scsi3_emulate_pro_register+0x73c/0x900 [target_core_mod] ... iscsi_target_rx_thread+0xef/0x1d0 [iscsi_target_mod] With a single-page parameter list the buffer is a kmap() direct mapping, so the over-read continues into the physically adjacent page instead of faulting. snprintf("%s") then copies whatever follows the ISID in memory into pr_reg_isid, and PR IN READ FULL STATUS reports the registration back to any initiator, turning the over-read into an info leak of kernel heap contents. Reproduced with a 4096-byte parameter list whose last TransportID ends at the end of the buffer with a 4-byte ISID and no NUL, interleaved with I/O to populate adjacent pages: the READ FULL STATUS response returned the ISID as "0xleak" followed by raw bytes that were not part of the parameter list. The snprintf() into pr_reg_isid[PR_REG_ISID_LEN] caps the echoed ISID at 15 characters, so at most 11 bytes past the buffer are leaked per command, but the PR OUT command is not rate limited. Any initiator that can send PR OUT to an iSCSI-exported LUN can trigger either variant, including a guest via vhost-scsi. Require 8 bytes to remain after the ",i,0x" separator, and a NUL inside the rest of the descriptor, before the ISID pointer is returned. REGISTER AND MOVE fails with TCM_INVALID_PARAMETER_LIST; on SPEC_I_PT no target port claims the malformed TransportID, and the command fails the same way.

t: drm/loongson: Fix double free on BO initialization failure
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/loongson: Fix double free on BO initialization failure If ttm_bo_init_validate() fails, it drops the buffer object's reference and cleans it up through the supplied destroy callback. lsdc_bo_destroy() releases the GEM object and frees the enclosing lsdc_bo, so freeing it again in lsdc_bo_create() causes a double free on a synchronous failure path. Let TTM own the cleanup after initialization has started and return the error directly. Keep the explicit free on drm_gem_object_init() failure, which occurs before ownership is passed to TTM. Tested on LS7A2000 by making drm_vma_offset_add() return -ENOSPC for one selected dumb-buffer creation. The error reached userspace, the destroy callback ran once, and no handle was published or tracked BO retained. Normal buffer creation, zeroing, mapping, readback and release passed. AI assistance was used for the ownership analysis, fix, fault-injection tools, build and test execution.

t: drm/loongson: Handle buffer mapping failures when clearing a BO
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/loongson: Handle buffer mapping failures when clearing a BO lsdc_bo_clear() ignores the return value from lsdc_bo_kmap() and writes to lbo->kptr unconditionally. When the first mapping of a newly allocated buffer fails, kptr is still NULL and the subsequent memset accesses it. Return the mapping error without touching the buffer and propagate it from lsdc_gem_object_create(). Install the GEM object functions before clearing so that drm_gem_object_put() can release the buffer correctly on failure. Do not add the failed object to the tracking list or return an uncleared buffer to the caller. Imported buffers still skip clearing, and successfully mapped buffers are cleared and unmapped as before. Tested on LS7A2000 with a one-shot range error in ttm_bo_kmap(). Its -EINVAL return reached userspace, the object was destroyed once, and no GEM handle was published. Normal create/map/zero/write/read/close cycles passed, with the tracked BO count and VRAM usage unchanged. AI assistance was used for the lifetime analysis, fix, fault-injection tools, build and test execution.

t: bpf: Fix skb_pull() BUG in __bpf_redirect_neigh()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: bpf: Fix skb_pull() BUG in __bpf_redirect_neigh() The issue: This is a follow-up to the short link-layer header fixes from Eric. After vlan pop_eth, a privileged SCHED_ACT BPF program can call bpf_skb_change_head(skb, 1, 0) and then bpf_redirect_neigh(). __bpf_redirect_neigh() calls skb_pull(skb, sizeof(*ethh)) after checking only that mac_header < network_header. Nothing verifies that the MAC header is long enough, that it is linear, or that the IP header the redirect goes on to read is linear either. A SCHED_ACT BPF program can do: bpf_skb_change_head(skb, 1, 0); bpf_redirect_neigh(lo, NULL, 0, 0); after vlan pop_eth. The skb then has mac_len == 1 and only one byte of linear data; skb_pull(ETH_HLEN) trips the skb->len < skb->data_len BUG in __skb_pull(): kernel BUG at ./include/linux/skbuff.h:2839! RIP: skb_pull+0x40/0x50 Call Trace: skb_do_redirect -> packet_xmit -> packet_sendmsg Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception in interrupt The v4 and v6 paths read ip_hdr() and ipv6_hdr() as soon as the MAC header is gone. On the AF_PACKET frame below that leaves headlen == 0 after the pull, so the network header sits at skb->tail and the route lookup reads ip4h->protocol, ip4h->saddr and ip4h->daddr past the linear area. The Fix: Use skb_network_offset(), which is the MAC header span, instead of skb->mac_len. mac_len is zero for locally generated tc egress and netkit packets, while the span still rejects the one-byte header produced by pop_eth + bpf_skb_change_head(skb, 1, 0). The single check also covers the mac_header >= network_header test it replaces. Use pskb_may_pull() to make the Ethernet header linear before it is read or pulled, and to make the IP header linear in both the v4 and the v6 path before ip_hdr()/ipv6_hdr() is read. The header pointers are taken after the pull, since pskb_may_pull() may reallocate skb->head. Conditions to recreate the bug: On x86-64 with 4 KiB pages, enable CONFIG_PACKET, CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL, CONFIG_NET_SCH_INGRESS, CONFIG_NET_CLS_MATCHALL, CONFIG_NET_ACT_VLAN and CONFIG_NET_ACT_BPF. Run as root with BPF loading, network administration and raw-packet privileges. Bring lo up and attach a SCHED_ACT program that calls bpf_skb_change_head(skb, 1, 0), then returns bpf_redirect_neigh(skb->ifindex, NULL, 0, 0): ip link set lo up tc qdisc add dev lo clsact tc filter add dev lo egress matchall action vlan pop_eth pipe \ action bpf object-file neigh_chghead.o section action Send an untagged ETH_P_IP frame of ETH_HLEN + 8192 bytes through an AF_PACKET/SOCK_RAW socket bound to lo, without PACKET_VNET_HDR or PACKET_QDISC_BYPASS. Use a unicast destination MAC. The sender's skb has a 14-byte linear Ethernet prefix and a fragmented payload; pop_eth removes that prefix and change_head restores only one linear byte. The unfixed neighbor redirect then tries to pull 14 bytes and BUGs. Sending the same frame without pop_eth and change_head leaves the IP header in the frags, which is the route lookup reading past skb->tail.

t: ksmbd: require DELETE access for delete-on-close opens
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: require DELETE access for delete-on-close opens smb2_open() accepts FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE on an existing file without DELETE in DesiredAccess. When the request asks only for FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES or READ_CONTROL, it also skips inode_permission() and the parent directory MAY_WRITE | MAY_EXEC check that delete-on-close is meant to get. The file is then marked for deletion by a caller who could not delete it. The unlink happens later, in __ksmbd_inode_close(), when the last handle on the inode is closed, and it runs with the credentials of that handle. If the caller closes last, the unlink fails. If another user who can write the parent directory, such as the file's owner, still has the file open, the file is deleted when that user closes it. Until then new opens of the file fail with STATUS_DELETE_PENDING. So a user with only search permission on a directory can delete a file in it, or block opens of it, while the owner has it open. A MAXIMUM_ALLOWED open that also requests DELETE has the same problem. The requested access is replaced with the maximal access, which does not include DELETE when the caller cannot write the parent directory, and the later permission checks are skipped as already done. MS-FSA 2.1.5.1 requires an open with FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE and without DELETE in DesiredAccess to fail with STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER, and Samba does the same. Add that check to the CreateOptions validation, using the generic-mapped DesiredAccess so that GENERIC_ALL still qualifies. This also refuses MAXIMUM_ALLOWED with FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE but no explicit DELETE, as MS-FSA and Samba do. When MAXIMUM_ALLOWED is requested with DELETE but the maximal access does not include DELETE, fail with STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED. With DELETE requested, delete-on-close opens go through the existing parent directory check.

t: ksmbd: enforce the read-only share flag when creating a stream
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: enforce the read-only share flag when creating a stream When a share is read-only, smb2_open() rejects opens that would create or truncate a file. Creating a named stream on an existing file with streams_xattr sets neither O_CREAT nor O_TRUNC, so it passes this check, and smb2_set_stream_name_xattr() then creates the stream. On a Time Machine share, opening a missing AFP_AfpInfo stream also writes one. A user who can write a file at the filesystem level can therefore add streams to it through a read-only share. Do not create a stream or synthesize AFP_AfpInfo when the share is not writable. Existing streams still open normally, and a missing stream opened with FILE_OPEN still returns STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_NOT_FOUND.

t: ksmbd: revert fsids on durable reconnect and replay failure
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: revert fsids on durable reconnect and replay failure On a durable handle reconnect or a request replay, smb2_open() switches to the SMB user's fsids before calling ksmbd_vfs_getattr(). If that call fails, the code jumps to err_out2 and skips ksmbd_revert_fsids() at err_out1. The user's credentials then stay installed on the shared ksmbd worker. Later work on that worker, including other users' requests, runs with the first user's fsuid, fsgid and supplementary groups. ksmbd_free_work_struct() also warns, because work->saved_cred is still set. Jump to err_out1 instead. No path is held at this point, so skipping the path_put() at err_out is correct.

t: ksmbd: fix NULL pointer dereference in session_user_name() and session_account_type()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix NULL pointer dereference in session_user_name() and session_account_type() session_user_name() and session_account_type() dereference session->user without checking for NULL. A session can be published and exposed via the procfs session interface before authentication completes, during which session->user is NULL: show_proc_session() -> session_user_name(sess) -> user_guest(session->user) -> NULL->flags -> oops Guard both functions by treating a NULL session->user as an explicit not-yet-authenticated state rather than dereferencing it.

t: ASoC: SOF: Intel: hda-sdw-bpt: Stop active DMA before closing BPT streams
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ASoC: SOF: Intel: hda-sdw-bpt: Stop active DMA before closing BPT streams When sdw_enable_stream() fails in intel_ace2x_bpt_send_async() after hda_sdw_bpt_send_async() has already started the TX and RX DMA streams, intel_ace2x_bpt_close_stream() invokes hda_sdw_bpt_close() directly without calling hda_sdw_bpt_wait(). As a result, hda_sdw_bpt_dma_deprepare() tears down the DMA buffers and BDL while the DMA hardware is still running. Disable any running TX or RX BPT DMA stream at the start of hda_sdw_bpt_close() before unmapping channels and depreparing DMA resources.

t: x86/bugs: Select the BHI mitigation based on the attack vector properly
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: x86/bugs: Select the BHI mitigation based on the attack vector properly The BHI mitigation selection is inconsistent with the documentation (attack_vector_controls.rst), which lists BHI under both the user->kernel and guest->host attack vectors. bhi_select_mitigation() only enables it when CPU_MITIGATE_GUEST_HOST is set; otherwise it selects BHI_MITIGATION_OFF, even if CPU_MITIGATE_USER_KERNEL is set. As a result, a kernel compiled with KVM disabled gets BHI automatically disabled, since CPU_MITIGATE_GUEST_HOST defaults to off without KVM. This is a bug, given that CPU_MITIGATE_USER_KERNEL still needs it: on affected Intel CPUs these kernels lose BHI_DIS_S or the BHB clearing loop by default. Booting with mitigations=auto,no_guest_host has the same effect. Select BHI_MITIGATION_ON whenever user->kernel is mitigated, and keep BHI_MITIGATION_VMEXIT_ONLY for the guest->host-only case. [ bp: Clarify commit title. ]

t: net: atl1c: drop oversized RX frames instead of panicking
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net: atl1c: drop oversized RX frames instead of panicking atl1c sizes its receive buffers from the netdev MTU plus a fixed set of L2 overheads, which comes to 1522 bytes at the default MTU.
