A link partner that sends a longer frame - in practice a MikroTik CCR2004-1G-2XS-PCIe, whose RouterOS side defaults to l2mtu 1600 while the host stays at MTU 1500 - makes the length reported by the RX return descriptor exceed what the hardware wrote, and skb_put() then either includes bytes that were never received or trips skb_over_panic and takes the host down. Compare the descriptor length against buffer_info->length, the length the hardware was given, rather than against skb_tailroom(): the skb carries 64 bytes of slack for the DMA erratum, so tailroom is larger than the DMA buffer and a frame in between would pass the check and still be delivered with a tail the device never wrote. The same test rejects frames shorter than ETH_HLEN + ETH_FCS_LEN; before this change a reported length below ETH_FCS_LEN underflowed in skb_put(). The frame is dropped with kfree_skb_reason(SKB_DROP_REASON_PKT_TOO_BIG) so drop_monitor and the kfree_skb tracepoint see it, and counted through dev_core_stats_rx_dropped_inc(), which survives atl1c_get_stats() overwriting the hardware counters on every read. It also counts as work: atl1c_clean_rfd() has already recycled the RFD, and the refill at the end of the poll only runs when work_done is non-zero, so sustained oversized traffic would otherwise drain the ring and stop RX. Tested on a MikroTik CCR2004-1G-2XS-PCIe (4x AR8151) in a Proxmox VE host, with atl1c built from a DKMS tree carrying this change: the l2mtu-1600 traffic that panics the stock driver is dropped and counted with the patch applied, and received normally once the host MTU is raised to match. This complements commit 36c2009d90f2 ("net: atl1c: fix soft lockup on out-of-range tpd_cons read"), which fixed the TX side of the same "host dies while the card resets" problem.

t: ksmbd: grant a POSIX ACL group entry only to the group's members
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: grant a POSIX ACL group entry only to the group's members When no ACE of the DACL matches the caller, Everyone or Authenticated Users, smb_check_perm_dacl() falls back to the file's POSIX ACL. It takes the first ACL_USER or ACL_GROUP entry whose id equals the caller's uid. For ACL_GROUP, this compares a gid with the caller's uid. A numerical match grants the group's permissions even when the caller is not a member. Match a group entry only when the caller is also in the group.

t: mm/mempolicy: charge shared policy nodes
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/mempolicy: charge shared policy nodes Any local user can bypass memory.max with mbind() on a tmpfs file, and allocate unbounded kernel memory. mbind() sets a NUMA memory policy for a range of a mapping. If the mapping is of a shmem and friends, the kernel also stores the policy on the inode, in a tree with one entry per range of the file. Each mbind() on a single page of a mapping can add one shared policy node (struct sp_node) and one struct mempolicy to that tree. They outlive the mapping and stay around until the inode is destroyed. The tree is not bounded by the file size, so the file can be empty. Memory that user space can allocate must be charged to a memory cgroup. A slab cache does that for all of its objects if it is created with SLAB_ACCOUNT. numa_policy_init() creates the slab caches for both structs without SLAB_ACCOUNT, so they are not charged to any cgroup. Reproduced with mbind() on single pages of an empty tmpfs file, from a cgroup with memory.max=8M: the global OOM killer killed tasks owned by root, and the machine panicked. Fix this by creating both caches with SLAB_ACCOUNT. This change implies that mbind() can now fail when running into memcg limits. Further, the policy_cache also serves task and VMA policies, so they are similarly accounted now. Note that per-file limits are not really helpful, as the user could simply use many files; having limits per user is tricky as well. Fix generated by an LLM and submitted by Chris Mason in private. [ david: smaller description tweaks ]

t: tmpfs: keep the quota soft limits of an unused id
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: tmpfs: keep the quota soft limits of an unused id When the last reference to a dquot goes away, shmem_release_dquot() stores its limits in the rb tree of the mount, unless shmem_is_empty_dquot() says that there is nothing worth storing. That function looks at the usage and at the two hard limits only. So if the administrator sets nothing but soft limits for an id that owns no file yet, the entry is thrown away as soon as the dquot that Q_SETQUOTA used is released, and the id never gets to see a limit. To fix it, compare the soft limits as well: an entry can be empty only if both soft limits are zero as well, which is exactly what shmem_acquire_dquot() sets for a new entry. Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private. [ david: slightly adjusted description ]

t: mm/shmem: stop retrying folios that cannot be split
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: stop retrying folios that cannot be split A fault or collapse can insert a large folio crossing EOF after shmem_undo_range() has handled the boundary folios. If splitting that folio fails, truncate_inode_partial_folio() retains it when it is dirty. The final scan then repeatedly finds it because it restarts from an unchanged start. Truncation keeps the inode lock and ignores fatal signals while looping. A concurrent unlink() can then block other directory operations while holding the directory lock and waiting for the file's lock. Advance start past the retained folio, whose truncated part has already been zeroed. Do not move start backwards if the failed split has shrunk the folio. Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private. [ david: split fixes, simplify descriptions, adjust comments ]

t: mm/shmem: fix truncate hang in large swap entry
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: fix truncate hang in large swap entry Truncating a tmpfs file or memfd to a page-aligned size inside a large swap entry can loop indefinitely in shmem_undo_range(). The task holds the inode lock and cannot be killed. A large swap entry represents a whole swapped-out folio. For example, truncate a file whose pages 0-7 share one swap entry to four pages: [ 0 1 2 3 | 4 5 6 7 ] keep | discard ^ new EOF, start = 4 i_size has already been updated when boundary handling asks shmem_get_partial_folio() for page 4. Since it is swapped out, the helper calls shmem_get_folio() with SGP_READ. That rejects page 4 with -EINVAL because its starting offset equals i_size. Nothing is read back. The final scan cannot free the entry without losing pages 0-3. It skips it, restarts from start = 4, and finds it again indefinitely. An unaligned truncate avoids this particular failure because the requested page starts below i_size. Folios already in the page-cache cannot trigger it as the direct lookup will return them beyond EOF. Fix it by letting shmem_get_partial_folio() call shmem_swapin_folio() directly for swap entries. This bypasses the read path's i_size check, allowing the existing boundary handling to zero and split the folio. If swap-in returns a smaller folio, it also splits the swap entry so the final scan can free the entries beyond EOF. Retry the lookup if the entry changes during swap-in. Handling swap-in allocation failures remains broken and is unchanged by this commit. Even when shmem_swapin_folio() correctly returns -ENOMEM instead of -EEXIST, shmem_get_partial_folio() returns NULL and shmem_undo_range() skips boundary handling. If the large swap entry remains intact, truncation can still loop in the final scan, while hole punching can return without zeroing the boundary. This may read an entire large folio back from swap while holding i_rwsem, only to discard part of it. Avoiding that I/O would require splitting both the swap entry and any large folio still in the swap cache. That, however, is much bigger work.

t: mm/shmem: preserve allocation errors when swapping in large entries
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: preserve allocation errors when swapping in large entries shmem_swapin_folio() adjusts swap to the requested slot within a large swap entry before allocating a folio. If allocation or charging fails, the error path compares this adjusted value with the original entry still stored in the XArray in shmem_confirm_swap(). Unless the index is at the start of the entry, this turns -ENOMEM into -EEXIST even though nothing changed. The caller retries -EEXIST, so persistent allocation failures can leave the task spinning instead of returning the error. Restore swap to index_entry on allocation failure so the existing error path checks the original entry. This preserves the allocation error if the entry is unchanged and still retries if it changed concurrently.

t: mm/shmem: fix truncate loop after boundary swapin failure
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: fix truncate loop after boundary swapin failure If swapping in a large entry at the new EOF fails, shmem_undo_range() leaves the entry in place. Its final scan skips the entry, then restarts from the same start index and finds it again. Truncation can loop forever while holding i_rwsem. Advance start past the skipped entry so that a restarted scan can finish, as we already do for folios that cannot be split. Note that this does not fix the missing zeroing when boundary swapin fails, it merely prevents the endless loop.

t: mm/shmem: fix accounting of swapin-error markers
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: fix accounting of swapin-error markers A failed swap read replaces the swap entry with a swapin-error marker in the page-cache and subtracts its pages from "alloced" and "swapped"; however, it leaves their block charge in place. Removing the marker during truncate then subtracts from "swapped" again. This can underflow the counters or make swapped reach zero while other pages remain swapped out, causing swapoff to loop without finding them. When installing the marker, subtract only from "swapped" and let shmem_recalc_inode() reduce "alloced" and release the block charge. Make shmem_free_swap() report successful removal separately from the number of swap pages freed, so removing a swapin-error marker does not subtract from "swapped" again. It's a bit confusing, but replacing a swapped out page by a swapin-error marker in shmem_set_folio_swapin_error() behaves as follows: Initially: alloced=1, swapped=1, nrpages=0 Calling shmem_recalc_inode(inode, 0, -1) -> swapped = 0 -> freed = 1 - 0 - 0 = 1 -> alloced -= freed -> alloced=0, swapped=0, block charge released

t: mm/mglru: don't use stack pointers when walking PUD and PMD tables
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/mglru: don't use stack pointers when walking PUD and PMD tables MGLRU passes stack copies of page-table entries in walk_pud_range() and walk_pmd_range() when walking to the next level. These copies can become stale when khugepaged or MADV_DONTNEED (CONFIG_PT_RECLAIM) removes a PTE table concurrently. This pattern dates back to commit bd74fdaea146 ("mm: multi-gen LRU: support page table walks"). Likely, earlier locking masked the latent bug. Later changes exposed it: commit 1d65b771bc08 ("mm/khugepaged: retract_page_tables() without mmap or vma lock") allowed concurrent retraction, and commit cf4a65539c13 ("memcg-v1: no need for memcg locking for MGLRU") dropped the walker's outer RCU protection. The fix is simple, so just fix the original commit so we don't have to speculate. To fix it, pass the actual PMD/PUD pointers. This restores the RCU-protected lookup and validation against the live PMD. Note that the PUD handling is required as well to handle folded page tables correctly in all cases. Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private. [ david: handle walk_pud_range() as well, clarify+simplify description, adjust Fixes: ]

t: mm/shmem: make shmem_file() check the file's inode
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: make shmem_file() check the file's inode shmem_file() only checks if file->f_mapping is a shmem mapping. This mapping can belong to another file, however, as with a Coda file backed by a tmpfs container after mmap(). So it does not guarantee that the file inode is an actual shmem inode. Seal handling and memfd preservation use this check before accessing shmem inode state, so they can access an inode of the wrong type. Let's make shmem_file() check the inode's file operations instead, to identify shmem inodes reliably. This will identify regular shmem inodes, including memfds and ordinary tmpfs files, independently of wrapper file operations. Use shmem_mapping() in collapse_file() instead to not change the behavior of collapse_file(): it operates on the page cache and uses mapping->host for shmem inode operations. Focusing on the file does not seem relevant.

t: mm/truncate: look again if a folio left the mapping
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/truncate: look again if a folio left the mapping invalidate_inode_pages2_range() skips a folio which no longer belongs to the mapping by the time it has got the folio lock, on the assumption that somebody else has removed it from the page cache. But the folio may have been replaced, and then there is a new folio with the same data at that index. For most cases, like folio migration, that is impossible. However, collapse_file() only checks the refcount of the old folios, under the i_pages lock, and relies on their folio locks from there on. That works for users which repeat the lookup when they find folio->mapping changed. The following scenario is, however, possible: CPU0 pwrite(O_DIRECT) CPU1 collapse_file() kiocb_invalidate_pages() read the folio (old data), lock it refcount check the write completes copy to new_folio kiocb_invalidate_post_direct_write() find_get_entries() -> old folio xas_store(new_folio) folio->mapping = NULL folio_unlock(folio) folio_lock() folio->mapping != mapping -> continue In that scenario, the collapsed folio with the data from before the write stays in the page cache after the write has returned. This used to be impossible, as khugepaged only collapsed files that nobody had open for writing. Restart the lookup at that index, like shmem_undo_range() does. The same problem seems to exist in truncate_inode_pages_range() as well when truncate_inode_folio() fails, so handle it there as well, but slightly differently: simply check once more through find_get_entries().

t: mm/filemap: read mapping->a_ops->free_folio under i_lock
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/filemap: read mapping->a_ops->free_folio under i_lock memory_failure() -> ... -> filemap_remove_folio() can read mapping->a_ops after the inode has been freed. Once the folio is deleted from the pagecache it no longer pins the mapping, so after i_lock is dropped e.g., a concurrent final iput() can evict and free the inode before filemap_free_folio() looks up mapping->a_ops->free_folio. Most callers hold a reference on the inode, but not all. Documentation/filesystems/vfs.rst explicitly states that ->free_folio() must not assume the original address_space mapping still exists. Fix it by loading ->free_folio while i_lock is still held, similar to what folio_unmap_invalidate() does. Inline filemap_free_folio() into its remaining caller such that delete_from_page_cache_batch() also just loads the callback before dropping the i_lock. The bug was found by code inspection and has not been reproduced. Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private. [ david: get rid of filemap_free_folio() entirely; improve patch description ]

t: mm/filemap: don't lose a folio lock wakeup to a signal
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/filemap: don't lose a folio lock wakeup to a signal An exclusive waiter in folio_wait_bit_common() can leave the wait loop because of a fatal signal, then be woken by folio_unlock() before finish_wait(). If the waker did not hand over the lock, the waiter returns -EINTR without trying to acquire it. folio_wake_bit() stops after waking the first exclusive waiter, so this loses the wakeup and can leave other waiters asleep indefinitely on an unlocked folio. After finish_wait(), let a waiter woken without a lock handoff try once more to acquire the lock. If successful, return success so the caller's eventual unlock wakes the next waiter. Otherwise, the current lock owner will do so. Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private. [ david: clarify and simplify comment + description ]

t: mm/filemap: finish fault cleanup before dropping the fault lock
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/filemap: finish fault cleanup before dropping the fault lock On a retried fault, a fatal signal interrupting the folio lock wait makes lock_folio_maybe_drop_mmap() drop the fault lock without pinning the file. However, filemap_fault() may still need to release mapping->invalidate_lock. A concurrent munmap() can release the last file reference and free the mapping before that unlock. Defer dropping the fault lock to filemap_fault()'s retry cleanup, after releasing invalidate_lock. If the fault lock was already dropped for I/O, release the existing file reference instead. Keep the fault lock held for FAULT_FLAG_RETRY_NOWAIT as before.

t: mm/rmap: handle device-exclusive entries in folio_referenced_one()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/rmap: handle device-exclusive entries in folio_referenced_one() page_vma_mapped_walk() can return non-present device-exclusive entries, but folio_referenced_one() passes them to PTE young-bit accessors that require present PTEs. We must neither call clear_flush_young_ptes_notify() nor folio_pte_batch() with non-present entries. For example, clearing the young bit on non-present PTEs can corrupt the entry: on arm64 PTE_AF overlaps the swap type, so clearing it turns a device-exclusive entry into an ordinary swap entry. folio_pte_batch() will VM_WARN_ON_FOLIO. Apply the same approach as the previous fixes to e.g., damon_ptep_mkold(): treat these entries as old from the CPU's perspective and obtain their young state through the MMU notifier. Skip PTE batching and MGLRU look-around for non-present entries, and don't modify non-present PTEs.

t: mm/huge_memory: fix list corruption when deferred_split_scan() races with deferred_split_folio()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/huge_memory: fix list corruption when deferred_split_scan() races with deferred_split_folio() Since the deferred split queue became a list_lru, the isolate callback moves the folios it took a reference on to an on-stack list, linked through folio->_deferred_list, and deferred_split_scan() takes them off that list with list_del_init() without holding the list_lru lock. deferred_split_folio() does not know about the on-stack list. It only holds the list_lru lock when it looks at the same list_head, and it can run for such a folio: a THP is queued when it is mapped, as a candidate for the underused check, and is queued "again" when a part of it gets unmapped: CPU0 deferred_split_scan() CPU1 deferred_split_folio() list_del_init(&folio->_deferred_list) next->prev = prev prev->next = next entry->next = entry list_lru_lock_irqsave() folio_set_partially_mapped() __list_lru_add() list_empty(item) -> true list_add_tail(item, &l->list) item->next = &l->list item->prev = tail entry->prev = entry The folio now sits on the list_lru with ->prev pointing to itself. The next removal leaves the neighbours pointing to it, and they still do so after the folio has been freed. With CONFIG_DEBUG_LIST: list_del corruption. prev->next should be ffd4000000270090, but was ffd4000000278090. (prev=ffd4000000270090) Fix it by grabbing the lock around list_del_init() so deferred_split_folio() cannot race with it.

t: mm/huge_memory: properly handle refcounted PUD mappings on fork
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/huge_memory: properly handle refcounted PUD mappings on fork copy_huge_pud() copies device-DAX entries without taking a folio reference or updating mapcounts and the child's RSS. For example, MADV_GUARD_INSTALL sets VM_MAYBE_GUARD on a device-DAX VMA, forcing copy_page_range() to traverse the whole VMA on fork. Any remaining huge PUDs are then copied without accounting for the new mappings. Unmapping them in the child decrements accounting that was never added. Use vm_normal_page_pud() to identify refcounted mappings. Take a folio reference and add the child's PUD rmap and RSS accounting before installing the copied entry. Pass src and dst VMAs consistently instead of src and dst MM. Move the TODO.

t: drm/v3d: Widen cache_clean_lock over the whole L2TCACTL sequence
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: drm/v3d: Widen cache_clean_lock over the whole L2TCACTL sequence v3d_clean_caches() and v3d_flush_l2t() both write the single L2TCACTL register and poll its status bits. The mutex cache_clean_lock exists to serialize them, but v3d_clean_caches() only took the lock around its final FLM_CLEAN write. These functions run concurrently: v3d_flush_l2t() is issued from the BIN/RENDER/CSD invalidate path while v3d_clean_caches() runs from the CACHE_CLEAN queue, and each queue's scheduler uses its own ordered workqueue, so their run_job callbacks execute in parallel. Because clean locked only its final write, a concurrent flush can write L2TCACTL during clean's unlocked phase. Both use non read-modify-write writes to the one register, so whichever lands last wins: clean's TMUWCF write can land on the flush's in-flight L2TFLS invalidate, triggering the GFXH-1897 hazard of writing L2TCACTL while a flush is pending. Hold cache_clean_lock across the entire L2TCACTL access sequence so it is fully mutually exclusive with v3d_flush_l2t(), which already takes the lock around its own write.

t: cipso: fix optlen corruption in cipso_v4_delopt()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: cipso: fix optlen corruption in cipso_v4_delopt() cipso_v4_delopt() recomputes the option length by walking the option buffer after the CIPSO option has been moved out. The walk then reads the stale bytes at the tail of the buffer as option data, and a crafted setsockopt(IP_OPTIONS) buffer can make it treat one of them as an option length, increasing opt->opt.optlen beyond the valid option data. The corrupted length stays on the socket and is later used as the copy length by getsockopt(IP_OPTIONS) and by the udp/raw/ping sendmsg paths, where it exceeds the size of the buffers they copy into. Compute the new length from the intact options before the move and subtract the CIPSO length, and fill the padding with IPOPT_END.

t: ntfs: don't allow compression on volumes with clusters larger than 4K
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ntfs: don't allow compression on volumes with clusters larger than 4K On a volume made with "mkntfs -c 8192", a user can set FILE_ATTR_COMPRESSED on an empty file through system.ntfs_attrib. Writing to the file and reading it back after dropping the page cache then crashes: BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in ntfs_read_compressed_block+0xa2c/0x2040 Read of size 8192 at addr ffff88804355a000 by task dd/106 The read path only handles clusters up to 4K. It copies each cluster out of a single page, and a compression block of 16 8K clusters does not fit in the 64K ntfs_compression_buffer. Loading an inode already rejects compressed data on such volumes. Reject the flag change the same way.

t: vhost-vdpa: fix pinned page leak in vhost_vdpa_pa_map() error path
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: vhost-vdpa: fix pinned page leak in vhost_vdpa_pa_map() error path When pin_user_pages() or vhost_vdpa_map() fails, vhost_vdpa_pa_map() is supposed to unpin the pages pinned after the last successfully mapped chunk, i.e. the range [map_pfn, last_pfn]. The unpin is guarded by nchunks, but nchunks is reset to 0 every time a chunk is mapped from inside the current page list, so a failure after any such boundary leaves that pending range pinned forever. With physically scattered memory nearly every page list contains a boundary, so the leak happens on practically every failed IOTLB update. The pending range is non-empty exactly when a page has been pinned, which last_pfn already tells us, so drop nchunks and test last_pfn.

t: vringh: bound top-level re-entry into indirect tables
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: vringh: bound top-level re-entry into indirect tables In __vringh_iov(), the F_INDIRECT branch descends into the indirect table and continues before the descriptor accounting runs. A top-level indirect descriptor is therefore never charged to count. If such a descriptor sets NEXT to point back at itself, returning from the indirect table resumes at the same top-level descriptor, which is again not counted, so the walk never makes forward progress. Because count stays flat and indirect_count is reset to 0 on every return to the top-level table, neither bound in the loop check trips. A guest can spin the vringh worker at 100% CPU inside __vringh_iov(), an uninterruptible host DoS. Move the descriptor accounting above the indirect switch so that a top-level indirect descriptor is charged one top-level traversal step before the walk descends into its table, bringing this re-entry under the existing vrh->vring.num bound. Each top-level descriptor is still charged at most one step and indirect_count still bounds a single table, so legitimate chains (including the multiple-indirect case in tools/virtio/vringh_test.c) stay within vring.num, while a cyclic indirect descriptor is now rejected with -ELOOP.

t: hwmon: (aquacomputer_d5next) reject short status reports
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: hwmon: (aquacomputer_d5next) reject short status reports The HID raw_event callback runs before HID core validates the received report length. aqc_raw_event() reads device-specific status fields at fixed offsets, including multi-byte values, without first ensuring that the received buffer contains every field. A truncated report can therefore cause out-of-bounds reads and update hwmon state with unrelated data. The required length differs between supported devices and cannot be derived from the HID report descriptor. Define the minimum length needed by each asynchronous status format, select it while configuring the device, and reject reports that do not contain the last field accessed by that format. Keep the published length zero until probe configuration is complete, which also excludes legacy devices whose status is retrieved through feature reports.

t: hwmon: chipcap2: fix IRQ teardown ordering
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: hwmon: chipcap2: fix IRQ teardown ordering The threaded IRQs are currently requested before the hwmon device is registered. Since devres releases resources in reverse order, the hwmon device is unregistered before the IRQs are freed during driver teardown. An IRQ may therefore still run after the hwmon device has been released and access the stale data->hwmon pointer. Separate IRQ discovery from IRQ registration so that the IRQ numbers and alarm visibility flags are initialized before registering the hwmon device while the IRQs are released before the hwmon device during devres cleanup.

t: hwmon: (lm87) Fix drvdata type confusion in vrm_show() and vrm_store()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: hwmon: (lm87) Fix drvdata type confusion in vrm_show() and vrm_store() When an LM87 or ADM1024 device is probed with VID support enabled, reading from or writing to the vrm sysfs attribute triggers a driver data type confusion in vrm_show() and vrm_store() in drivers/hwmon/lm87.c. In lm87_probe(), the driver stores the struct lm87_data pointer on the I2C client via i2c_set_clientdata() and passes the struct i2c_client pointer as the drvdata argument to devm_hwmon_device_register_with_groups(), which attaches the attribute groups to the registered hwmon device with client as its driver_data. Unlike the other sysfs callbacks that retrieve client via dev_get_drvdata() and then obtain data via i2c_get_clientdata(), vrm_show() and vrm_store() assign dev_get_drvdata(dev) directly to struct lm87_data *. Dereferencing data->vrm therefore accesses the struct i2c_client instance at offsetof(struct lm87_data, vrm), causing vrm_show() to leak an unrelated byte from struct i2c_client to userspace and vrm_store() to corrupt a byte within struct i2c_client while failing to update the actual VRM value. Fix the problem by assigning the return value from dev_get_drvdata(dev) to struct i2c_client *client and using i2c_get_clientdata() to get the actual client data.

t: hwmon: (peci/dimmtemp) Fix devres leak and UAF on concurrent unbind
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: hwmon: (peci/dimmtemp) Fix devres leak and UAF on concurrent unbind When a peci_dimmtemp device is unbound concurrently with its delayed initialization work (detect_work), newly allocated devm resources and the hwmon device are leaked, leading to a use-after-free when reading the lingering hwmon sysfs attributes. In peci_dimmtemp_probe(), detect_work is registered for cancellation via devm_delayed_work_autocancel(). During driver detach, devres_release_all() first moves all existing entries from dev->devres_head onto a local todo list before invoking their release callbacks in reverse order. If create_dimm_temp_info_delayed() is already running when devm_delayed_work_drop() calls cancel_delayed_work_sync(), create_dimm_temp_info() can allocate dimmtemp_label strings via devm_kzalloc()/devm_kasprintf() and register the hwmon device via devm_hwmon_device_register_with_info(), appending new devres entries to the now-empty dev->devres_head. Once the work finishes, devres_release_all() frees priv and priv->name from the local todo list without re-evaluating dev->devres_head, leaving the late devres allocations and registered hwmon device behind with a dangling priv pointer. Cancel detect_work synchronously in a driver .remove() callback instead of relying on devm_delayed_work_autocancel() so that the work is fully drained before devres_release_all() detaches dev->devres_head, allowing any devm resources registered by the delayed work to be released in proper reverse order. Also only schedule detect_work when check_populated_dimms() returns -EAGAIN so that probe failure paths do not leave delayed work pending.

t: hwmon: (pmbus/q54sj108a2) Add missing NULL pointer check
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: hwmon: (pmbus/q54sj108a2) Add missing NULL pointer check When CONFIG_DEBUG_FS is enabled and per-client PMBus debugfs directory creation fails during pmbus_do_probe(), q54sj108a2_probe() passes the NULL pointer returned by pmbus_get_debugfs_dir() to debugfs_create_dir() without validation, creating its debugfs directory at the debugfs root instead of under the client directory. If pmbus_init_debugfs() fails to create the client directory, data->debugfs is left as NULL or an ERR_PTR, which pmbus_get_debugfs_dir() converts to NULL. Passing a NULL parent to debugfs_create_dir() places q54sj108a2_dir in the root of the debugfs filesystem and populates it with attribute files whose private data pointers reference psu->debugfs_entries. Because this root-level directory is outside the client debugfs hierarchy, PMBus core cleanup does not remove it on device unbind, leaking the debugfs entries and causing a use-after-free of the devm-allocated struct q54sj108a2_data if the orphaned files are accessed via q54sj108a2_debugfs_read() or q54sj108a2_debugfs_write() after device removal. Fix the problem by adding the missing NULL pointer check.

t: hwmon: (coretemp) Set nr_cores only after core_data allocation succeeds
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: hwmon: (coretemp) Set nr_cores only after core_data allocation succeeds In init_temp_data(), pdata->nr_cores is populated from topology_num_cores_per_package() before allocating pdata->core_data. If that allocation fails, init_temp_data() returns NULL with pdata->core_data still NULL and pdata->nr_cores set to a positive value. coretemp_add_core() logs the error without failing coretemp_cpu_online(), so the CPU still comes online with pdata->hwmon_dev registered. When the CPU is later taken offline (or the module is unloaded), coretemp_cpu_offline() calls get_temp_data(pd, cpu), which loops up to pdata->nr_cores and dereferences the NULL pdata->core_data pointer. Store the core count in a local variable and assign pdata->nr_cores only after pdata->core_data is allocated, preserving the invariant that pdata->nr_cores is zero whenever pdata->core_data is NULL.

t: nvme-rdma: fix NULL queue->ctrl dereference on reconnect
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvme-rdma: fix NULL queue->ctrl dereference on reconnect Since commit 2a8513091d2f ("nvme-rdma: parallelize I/O queue allocation and startup"), a reconnect that gets more I/O queues than before grows the tag set before the new queues are set up. queue->ctrl is only set by nvme_rdma_setup_io_queues(), so I/O submitted in between reaches nvme_rdma_queue_rq() on a queue that was never allocated and dereferences a NULL queue->ctrl: BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 000000000000034c RIP: 0010:nvme_rdma_queue_rq+0x52/0xb90 Set queue->ctrl for every queue when allocating the controller. Such requests are then requeued like on any other queue that is not live.

t: nvme: Do not drop the cdev reference twice when cdev_device_add() fails
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvme: Do not drop the cdev reference twice when cdev_device_add() fails Since commit 9952f3882ecb ("nvme: fix cdev lifetime"), nvme_add_ns_cdev() and nvme_add_ns_head_cdev() take a reference to the namespace (or namespace head) before calling nvme_cdev_add(), to be dropped by the char device's release, nvme_cdev_rel(), and drop it themselves when nvme_cdev_add() fails. But when cdev_device_add() fails, nvme_cdev_add() has already put the device, and nvme_cdev_rel() has already dropped that reference: the caller drops it a second time. With one allocation failure injected into cdev_device_add() for a namespace on an NVMe over loop controller, deleting the controller gives, with native multipath: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in nvme_put_ns_head+0x21/0x140 Write of size 4 at addr ff1100000a4ea078 by task init/1 nvme_put_ns_head nvme_put_ns nvme_remove_namespaces nvme_do_delete_ctrl nvme_delete_ctrl_sync nvme_sysfs_delete Freed by task 1: kfree nvme_ns_remove nvme_remove_namespaces refcount_t: underflow; use-after-free. Take the reference in nvme_cdev_add() instead, right before cdev_device_add(), and let the callers neither take nor drop it. Add nvme_is_ns_cdev() for the check that nvme_cdev_rel() and nvme_cdev_add() now share.

t: KVM: x86/mmu: Conditionally resched when retrying gPTE walk on A/D update failure
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86/mmu: Conditionally resched when retrying gPTE walk on A/D update failure Conditionally reschedule when retrying a guest PTE walk because the CMPXCHG to update A/D bits failed, e.g. because a different task/vCPU modified the relevant gPTEs. On kernels without involuntary preemption of some kind, a misbehaving guest can "capture" a pCPU effectively indefinitely and trigger soft lockups by continuously modifying its gPTEs such that the result of the walk is remains valid.

t: KVM: x86: Conditionally resched when restarting REP string emulation
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86: Conditionally resched when restarting REP string emulation When restarting emulation, e.g. of a REP-prefixed string instruction, conditionally reschedule as emulating guest writes can be deceptively slow and expensive, e.g. when shadow paging is in use and each write can trigger write tracking. In a perfect world, restarting emulation (or not) would be less arbitrary, e.g. would honor not only host events (NEED_RESCHED, signals, etc.) but also guest events (e.g. by checking kvm_vcpu_has_events()). Unfortunately, as pointed out by Sashiko, pio_in_emulated()'s read-ahead logic is baked into the restart logic, as KVM relies on restarting emulation to drain the cache and avoid duplicate reads from the I/O port. I.e. re-entering the guest on kvm_vcpu_has_events() or __xfer_to_guest_mode_work_pending() would introduce architecturally-incorrect, guest-visible changes.

t: KVM: nVMX: Process each host MSR entry at most once when unwinding failed VM-Entry
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: nVMX: Process each host MSR entry at most once when unwinding failed VM-Entry Add a missing "break" in the inner for-loop of the open coded mess that unwinds MSRs back to the pre-VM-Enter state when VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME VM-Fails due to a consistency check that is caught by hardware but missed by KVM. I.e. move on to the next MSR in the VM-Entry load list after performing a write using a value found in the VM-Exit load list. Processing *every* matching entry in the VM-Exit load list makes the processing quadratic, which is problematic if the load lists are full of MSRs that are expensive to emulate. E.g. writing APIC_BASE triggers kvm_recalculate_apic_map() and a whole pile of unnecessary work. Functionally, arbitrarily restoring the value of the first matching entry is "fine", because none of this is architecturally correct: the load lists are never supposed to have been used in the first place. In practice, it's likely a moot point as no well-behaved VMM will have multiple, diverging entries in the load lists.

t: KVM: x86/mmu: Cap number of parent PTEs per SP at 1000 (the arbitrary rmap limit)
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86/mmu: Cap number of parent PTEs per SP at 1000 (the arbitrary rmap limit) When potentially reusing a shadow page, zap the shadow page if its number of parent PTEs exceeds KVM's (mostly) arbitrary rmap recycling threshold. Letting the guest create a (mostly) unbounded number of parent PTEs allows the guest to coerce KVM into creating lists containing millions of PTEs, effectively bounded only by the maximum number of shadow pages. Because PTE lists are simple singly linked lists, removal is O(n). Even worse, if a list is constructed just so, teardown can be O(n^2), e.g. if SPTEs are built such that zapping child SPTEs always zaps the last entry in the list. To cap things off, all paths that walk PTE lists do so while holding mmu_lock, without conditionally rescheduling. Using a doubly linked list would not address the issue, as removal would remain O(n) since KVM still wouldn't know where in the list to remove from. Removal could be made O(1) by storing a per-SPTE pointer, but that would largely defeat the purpose of reusing SPs, and would penalize well-behaved guests, especially for nested TDP where aliasing page tables is uncommon. So, cap the maximum number of parent PTEs at the rmap limit. In practice, well-behaved guests will likely never run afoul of the limit. E.g. when running Linux as L1 with TDP, the number of parent PTEs for a single SP tops out at under 200 (though undoubtedly obscure workloads can push it higher). Deliberately use a "greater than or equal" as opposed to rmap's strictly "greater than", as the rmap code checks the threshold immediately *after* inserting into the list, i.e. the limit is 1000 for rmaps, KVM just very briefly blows past it. Apply the check to both indirect and direct SPs, because while a fully direct MMU naturally limits the number of parent PTEs to '1', direct SPs in indirect MMUs have no such constraint. E.g. if the guest maps a huge PTE into many locations in its page tables, and KVM is backing the hugepage with a direct SP, i.e. with a series of smaller pages, then KVM could end up with a direct SP with many parents. Note, shadow_mmu_try_split_huge_pages() always restarts the rmap walk or bails entirely if it gets to the point where it tries to grab a SP, i.e. there is *no* pre-existing bug that would be tripped by zapping a SP and thus rmaps when getting a SP.

t: inet: frags: limit the truesize of a reassembly queue
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: inet: frags: limit the truesize of a reassembly queue The truesize of fragments in a reassembly queue is only bounded by the per netns ipfrag_high_thresh sysctl, which has no upper limit. inet_frag_reasm_finish() sums the truesize of all fragments in an int. If this sum reaches 2^32, it wraps, and the final sk_wmem_alloc adjustment of the socket owning the reassembled skb can cancel its own reference, leading to a use-after-free of this socket. This can be triggered from an unprivileged user/network namespace, raising ipfrag_high_thresh and using padded TUN packets, which keep a large truesize after being trimmed by ip_rcv_core(). Track the sum of the truesize of fragments in each queue, and refuse a fragment that would make it bigger than INT_MAX / 2. Callers kill the queue on this error. This bound is far above the needs of legitimate traffic.

t: ipv6: reject wrapped temporary address preferred lifetimes
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ipv6: reject wrapped temporary address preferred lifetimes ipv6_create_tempaddr() raises a temporary address's preferred lifetime to regen_advance + age + 1 when the configured lifetime is too short. The result is stored in a u32, while regen_advance and age are unsigned long. If the sum wraps or is truncated, the stored lifetime can still be less than or equal to regen_advance + age. addrconf_verify_rtnl() then sees the new address as due for regeneration and creates another one. Temporary addresses are not limited by max_addresses since commit 4b08a8f1bd8c ("ipv6: remove max_addresses check from ipv6_create_tempaddr"), so this can cause unbounded address growth. With dad_transmits set to -1, a baseline kernel reached 2859 loopback addresses in two seconds. After storing the adjusted lifetime, verify that it is still greater than regen_advance + age. Reject the new address if the check fails. On an x86-64 KASAN kernel, the normal configuration created three IPv6 addresses. The negative dad_transmits, positive multiplication overflow, and large retransmission-time cases each left only the loopback and public addresses. An i386 defconfig and an x86-64 allmodconfig both built addrconf.o with W=1.

t: mm/khugepaged: flush deferred unmaps before dropping a failed folio
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/khugepaged: flush deferred unmaps before dropping a failed folio collapse_file() can fail its reference-count or dirty-folio check after unmapping with TTU_BATCH_FLUSH. Both paths put back the isolated folio, then unlock it and drop the lookup reference before reaching the common try_to_unmap_flush(). The page-cache reference does not keep the folio stable once the lock is released. Another collapse can replace and free it. With its PTEs already gone, that collapse cannot flush the first task's per-task TLB batch, and retract_page_tables() skips short or unaligned VMAs. A CPU can therefore retain a user translation to the freed folio. This has been reproduced with unprivileged MADV_COLLAPSE on a memfd. Flush at out_unlock while the lookup reference and folio lock are still held. The common flush continues to cover the accumulated pagelist on both success and rollback, preserving batching on successful collapses.

t: mm: fix address wraparound when scanning large folio PTEs
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm: fix address wraparound when scanning large folio PTEs numa_rebuild_large_mapping() and do_swap_page() can be tricked into generating an address wraparound, crashing the kernel. All that's required is to map a tail page of a large folio close enough to the start/end of the address space to e.g., make unsigned long addr_start = addr - (nr << PAGE_SHIFT); to wrap around. Let's fix it by providing a better helper, folio_scan_range(), that takes care of staying within VMA and page table boundaries while handling possible wraparounds. There are some nasty details, like not being able to use pmd_addr_end() in this context. Add some helpful comments for these cases.

t: mm: memory: fix truncation removing mapped folios
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm: memory: fix truncation removing mapped folios Ayush reported an issue that shmem/tmpfs folios are still mapped when truncating them on production: " BUG: Bad page cache in process ... pfn:... page dumped because: still mapped when deleted " I reproduced the issue with Ayush's reproducer [1] with the latest mm-unstable branch, and I got the following crash info. From the dump message, we can see that truncate_inode_folio() is really trying to remove mapped folios, which is incorrect. " [ 189.171977] page: refcount:3 mapcount:1 mapping:00000000fe168ee1 index:0x3880 pfn:0x191647 [ 189.171995] memcg:ffff0000cc073d40 [ 189.171997] aops:shmem_aops ino:3c01 dentry name(?):"memfd:runsc-memory" [ 189.172006] flags: 0x17fffef0002022d(locked|referenced|uptodate|lru| workingset|swapbacked|node=0|zone=2|lastcpupid=0x3ffff) ....... [ 189.172017] page dumped because: VM_BUG_ON_FOLIO(folio_mapped(folio)) [ 189.172026] ------------[ cut here ]------------ [ 189.172027] kernel BUG at mm/filemap.c:155! [ 189.172057] Internal error: Oops - BUG: 00000000f2000800 [#1] SMP ....... [ 189.177721] CPU: 3 UID: 0 PID: 5521 Comm: repro Kdump: loaded Tainted: 7.3.0-rc4+ #277 PREEMPT(lazy) ....... [ 189.183986] Call trace: [ 189.184124] filemap_unaccount_folio+0xf0/0x1e8 (P) [ 189.184391] __filemap_remove_folio+0x34/0x160 [ 189.184633] filemap_remove_folio+0x4c/0xb0 [ 189.184859] truncate_inode_folio+0x34/0x58 [ 189.185087] shmem_undo_range+0x220/0x658 [ 189.185308] shmem_fallocate+0x2f0/0x470 [ 189.185527] vfs_fallocate+0x128/0x328 ...... [ 189.187078] el0t_64_sync+0x184/0x188 " After analysis, I believe the race exists between truncation and MADV_DONTNEED, and shmem's ->map_pages() merely makes the issue easier to reproduce. Since MADV_DONTNEED synchronously releases the pagetable page before calling tlb_flush_rmaps(), this could cause another thread's truncation to skip zap_pte_range() (due to pmd is none) but still observe the folio's mapcount as non-zero. A possible race scenario is as follows: CPU 0 CPU 1 shmem_fallocate madvise_dontneed_single_vma unmap_mapping_range ....... ...... (filemap_map_pages() remap folios) zap_pte_range truncate_inode_folio zap_empty_pte_table(pmd clear) unmap_mapping_folio ...... zap_pmd_range (saw pmd none, skip) filemap_remove_folio BUG_ON(folio_mapped) tlb_flush_rmaps(remove rmaps) To fix this issue, we should move the pmd clear operation (via zap_empty_pte_table()) to after tlb_flush_rmaps() and use sync_with_folio_pmd_zap() to sync with concurrent zapping, so that when we find a pmd_none() while unmapping a folio without holding the PTL, the folio's mappings are guaranteed to have been removed via tlb_flush_rmaps(). Meanwhile move the second pmd_none() check to where it belongs: if splitting zapped the PMD.

t: mm/page-writeback: avoid 32-bit overflow in dirty threshold shares
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/page-writeback: avoid 32-bit overflow in dirty threshold shares The ratios used by __wb_calc_thresh() are scaled to parts per million, but the threshold and ratio operands are unsigned long. On 32-bit kernels, their multiplication can wrap before the result is assigned to u64. For example, with a threshold of 25600 pages and the default maximum ratio of 1000000, wb_max_thresh becomes 4125 pages instead of 25600. The shared threshold and minimum share calculations can overflow in the same way, producing incorrect per-writeback dirty limits. Use a u64 threshold for the three ratio multiplications and div_u64() to retain the existing division order and rounding.

t: mm/hugetlb: fix mremap deadlock when PMD sharing is possible
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/hugetlb: fix mremap deadlock when PMD sharing is possible move_hugetlb_page_tables() holds the mapping's i_mmap_rwsem for write while moving hugetlb PTEs. This prevents races with truncation and protects huge_pmd_unshare(), but the move loop must not call helpers that can acquire the same rwsem for read. huge_pte_alloc() can do that when the destination can use PMD sharing: it may call huge_pmd_share(), which takes i_mmap_rwsem for read while searching for a shareable PMD table. Calling it while the move path already holds i_mmap_rwsem for write can deadlock. Avoid that path for PMD-sized hugetlb mappings that can use PMD sharing. Instead of allocating or sharing the destination page table while moving, zap the source range and let the destination fault path populate or share the PMD lazily. Reuse the hugetlb unmap logic for the source-side zap by splitting the core loop out of __unmap_hugepage_range(). The wrapper keeps the existing tlb_start_vma(), tlb_end_vma() and huge_pmd_unshare_flush() behavior, while move_hugetlb_page_tables() can reuse the unmap loop with its existing mmu_gather.

t: mm/vma: write lock source VMA before duplicating it in __split_vma()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/vma: write lock source VMA before duplicating it in __split_vma() __split_vma() duplicates the source VMA before taking its VMA write lock, and until the VMA is write-locked, a concurrent thread might set VMA_MAYBE_GUARD_BIT, resulting in the duplication missing the flag. If this happens, then fork may fail to duplicate guard markers and, if a file-backed mapping, THP collapse may also discard the markers. Resolve this by taking the VMA write lock before vm_area_dup() and, since all callers of vm_area_dup() now hold the VMA write lock, assert that this is the case there, and add a comment to explain why it's needed. [ljs@kernel.org: add VMA write assert in vm_area_dup(), commit message touchup]

t: mm/ksm: fix userfaultfd protection during merge and unmerge
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/ksm: fix userfaultfd protection during merge and unmerge KSM loses userfaultfd protection when replace_page() builds a new PTE from vma->vm_page_prot. Dropping its uffd bit lets a subsequent write go through ordinary COW instead of userfaultfd write protection handling. For RWP, a merged page also becomes readable without faulting. Keeping the uffd bit and restoring PAGE_NONE fixes merging, but we also have to handle unmerging. An existing KSM page can be protected with RWP before MADV_UNMERGEABLE, so unmerging already needs fixing independently of preserving RWP during merging. Unsharing replaces a shared page with a private one and should leave userfaultfd protection in place, as do_wp_page() already does for write protection. Currently, an unshare fault reaches do_uffd_rwp() before it can proceed to do_wp_page(). - With synchronous RWP, handle_userfault() returns VM_FAULT_SIGBUS. break_ksm() then reports success with a KSM page still merged. - With asynchronous RWP, protection is cleared before unsharing. Preserve the uffd bit when merging, and restore PAGE_NONE for RWP. Let FAULT_FLAG_UNSHARE skip RWP fault handling and keep PAGE_NONE on each private copy as well. Unsharing can then complete with RWP still armed for a subsequent access.

t: mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: map the shared tail page writable
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: map the shared tail page writable page_ref_add_unless_zero() reads the refcount and then updates it with a cmpxchg. A lockless get, such as a page cache lookup or a PFN scanner, can read a non-zero refcount from a page that is then freed and reused as a hugetlb tail page. If HVO remaps its struct page to the shared tail page in between, the cmpxchg writes to read-only vmemmap: CPU0 (lockless get) CPU1 c = atomic_read(&page->_refcount) page freed page allocated as a hugetlb tail HVO remaps the struct page RO try_cmpxchg(&page->_refcount, &c, c + 1) -> write fault on read-only vmemmap The refcount is zero by then and the compare fails, but a compare-and-swap instruction needs write access whether or not it succeeds. The kernel oopses when hugetlb pages are allocated at runtime with HVO enabled while a lockless get races with it. Commit bd225530a4c7 ("mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: fix race with speculative PFN walkers") closed the window with RCU on both sides. The RCU was removed together with fake heads, on the wrong belief that it was only needed for them. Map the shared tail page writable instead of restoring the RCU. Every struct page on it is a tail with a zero refcount, so a late cmpxchg fails and leaves the page unchanged. RCU would put rcu_read_lock() back around every get and synchronize_rcu() back into hugetlb allocation and freeing. The cost is the protection against stray writes to tail struct pages. The shared page is shared by all hugetlb folios of the same order in the zone, so such a write now corrupts all of them instead of oopsing. Bootmem folios optimized when the memmap is set up keep their tails read-only. Nothing does a lockless get on them before hugetlb takes them over.

t: mm/cma: accept memory of multi-range CMA areas
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/cma: accept memory of multi-range CMA areas Patch series "mm/cma: accept memory of CMA areas reserved with memblock_reserve()", v1. Pages of allocated CMA areas are released to the buddy allocator with __free_pages(), which does not check for unaccepted memory. This usually works because memblock accepts the memory it allocates. However, multi-range CMA areas, used by hugetlb_cma, and fixed CMA areas requested with cma=<size>@<base> are reserved with memblock_reserve() and their memory is never accepted. On TDX and SEV-SNP guests the first access to such a page is fatal. To ease the backporting, each case is addressed by a separate patch: - patch 1 accepts the memory of multi-range CMA areas - patch 2 does the same for the fixed CMA areas The second patch won't apply cleanly to 6.6 and 6.12, but I believe the stable team LLMs will take care of that :) This patch (of 2): On systems with unaccepted memory, memblock allocations accept the allocated range, but when cma_declare_contiguous_multi() uses open coded allocation of multiple ranges, it reserves them with memblock_reserve() and they are never accepted. These pages are released to the buddy allocator by cma_activate_area() with __free_pages() that does not check for unaccepted memory, so the first access to such a page in a TDX or SEV-SNP guest is fatal. Accept the memory of each range when it is reserved.

t: mm/cma: accept memory of CMA areas reserved at a fixed address
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/cma: accept memory of CMA areas reserved at a fixed address CMA areas allocated from memblock have their memory accepted by memblock_alloc_range_nid(), but areas reserved at a fixed address with memblock_reserve() are not. If a fixed CMA area is requested by the cma=<size>@<base> command line parameter, it may be in regular RAM and on TDX and SEV-SNP guests it must be accepted. Accept the memory of fixed CMA areas as well, so that all CMA areas are accepted regardless of how they were reserved.

t: mm: memcontrol: fix NULL pointer deref and UAF from high_work_func() on dying memcg
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm: memcontrol: fix NULL pointer deref and UAF from high_work_func() on dying memcg When memory.high is exceeded in non-task context, try_charge_memcg() schedules memcg->high_work without taking a reference on the memcg, and high_work_func() invokes reclaim_high() without pinning the memcg. With obj_cgroup reparenting, introduced in commit bf4f059954dc ("mm: memcg/slab: obj_cgroup API"), objects charged to a child memcg are reparented to its parent in mem_cgroup_css_offline() instead of holding a reference on the child until uncharged. Subsequent uncharges of those objects go to the parent, which can leave the child's memory use permanently above its high limit, so any later charge on the offlined memcg in non-task context schedules high_work. This was later widened from kernel memory to LRU folios when commit f1cf8d2f36dc ("mm: memcontrol: eliminate the problem of dying memory cgroup for LRU folios") converted LRU folios to use obj_cgroup reparenting. cancel_work_sync(&memcg->high_work) only runs at the end of teardown in mem_cgroup_css_free(), so high_work_func() can start or still be running reclaim_high() after mem_cgroup_css_released() or shrink_many() has called lru_gen_release_memcg() and unhashed lruvec->lrugen.list. If reclaim tries to rotate the memcg, lru_gen_rotate_memcg() dereferences a NULL pprev pointer. This issue is specific to MGLRU and was introduced with the memcg LRU in commit e4dde56cd208 ("mm: multi-gen LRU: per-node lru_gen_folio lists"). With either traditional LRU or MGLRU, css_free_rwork_fn() calls css_rstat_exit() which frees per-CPU rstat data before calling mem_cgroup_css_free(). If reclaim_high() is still running, rstat updates via mod_lruvec_state() -> __css_rstat_updated() cause a use-after-free on the per-CPU rstat data. This was introduced when commit 5da3bfa029d6 ("cgroup: use separate rstat trees for each subsystem") moved css_rstat_exit() ahead of ss->css_free(). Fix both problems by acquiring a reference with css_tryget_online() in high_work_func() before calling reclaim_high(), and by resetting memory.high and swap.high to PAGE_COUNTER_MAX in mem_cgroup_css_offline() so that charges via references on an offlined memcg do not trigger high_work on the dead child and skip checking live ancestors in try_charge_memcg(). Acquiring the reference in high_work_func() rather than before scheduling high_work is safe because mem_cgroup_css_free() calls irq_work_sync() and cancel_work_sync() which cancels pending work and waits for an already running high_work_func() to complete before mem_cgroup_free() frees the memcg. css_tryget_online() uses percpu_ref_tryget_live() and is safe to call after percpu_ref_exit() before the cgroup is freed unlike css_tryget(). Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc0000000000: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007] CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 27 Comm: kworker/1:0 Tainted: G B W 7.3.0-rc5-g2bba28e98578 #284 PREEMPT(full) Tainted: [B]=BAD_PAGE, [W]=WARN <-- Taint from lru_gen_rotate_memcg() VM_WARN_ON_ONCE Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS 1.17.0-debian-1.17.0-1 04/01/2014 Workqueue: events high_work_func RIP: 0010:lru_gen_rotate_memcg+0x1a3/0xe90 Call Trace: <TASK> ? read_ctrl_pos+0x22f/0x3f0 shrink_lruvec+0x16cb/0x1b80 ? ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30 ? lapic_next_event+0x15/0x20 ? clockevents_program_event+0x2bb/0x6f0 ? lapic_next_event+0x15/0x20 ? __pfx_shrink_lruvec+0x10/0x10 ? __pfx_clockevents_program_event+0x10/0x10 ? _raw_spin_lock+0x84/0xe0 ? __pfx__raw_spin_lock+0x10/0x10 ? kasan_save_stack+0x30/0x50 ? psi_group_change+0x381/0x740 ? __pfx_sched_clock_cpu+0x10/0x10 ? save_fpregs_to_fpstate+0xc4/0x2c0 ? finish_task_switch.isra.0+0x1de/0xac0 ? __schedule+0xf62/0x42c0 ? __pfx___schedule+0x10/0x10 ? __pfx___irq_work_queue_lo ---truncated---

t: ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after defragmenting a bucket
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after defragmenting a bucket ocfs2_xattr_set_entry_bucket() hands loc.xl_entry to ocfs2_xa_set() twice: once for the bucket as it stands, and, if that reports -ENOSPC, once more after ocfs2_defrag_xattr_bucket() has packed the name/value pairs down. Defragmenting ends by sorting the entry array on xe_name_hash. Buckets are kept sorted, so the sort only permutes entries that share a hash, but lib/sort.c is an unstable heapsort and it does permute them. loc.xl_entry is an address inside xh_entries[], so afterwards it denotes whichever entry landed in that slot rather than the one the search found. The second ocfs2_xa_set() then works on the wrong entry. Nothing on that path compares the entry's name with xi->xi_name, so what happens depends on how the two entries compare in size: ocfs2_xa_reuse_entry() trips its BUG_ON() when the padded name sizes differ, and otherwise the new value is written into the neighbouring attribute's value slot while the attribute being set is left untouched. setxattr() reports success either way. Remember the entry's hash before defragmenting and look the entry up again afterwards, the way ocfs2_xattr_bucket_find() does. An entry that cannot be found again means the bucket no longer holds what the search found, so fail with -EFSCORRUPTED rather than writing through the stale pointer.

t: ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after converting a block to a bucket
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after converting a block to a bucket ocfs2_xattr_create_index_block() turns a non-indexed xattr block into a tree by copying it into a bucket, and the copy sorts the entries: a block holds them in insertion order, a bucket by name hash. ocfs2_xattr_update_xattr_search() nevertheless relocates the caller's search by the index the entry had in the block, so unless the two orders agreed it points at an unrelated entry, and nothing between there and the write compares that entry's name with the one being set. Setting an xattr whose new value no longer fits the block arrives here with xs->not_found clear. The block gave up because ocfs2_xa_block_can_reuse() wants an exact namevalue size match, while ocfs2_xa_bucket_can_reuse() only wants an entry at least as large as the new one, so the bucket accepts a pair the block rejected and the update lands on whichever entry the sort left at that index. Equal padded name lengths get that other attribute's value replaced in place and its name left alone, so setxattr returns success while the attribute asked for keeps its old value. A longer one trips ocfs2_xa_reuse_entry()'s BUG_ON, and a shorter one is refused by the bucket as well, so ocfs2_xa_prepare_entry() wipes the entry and writes the new name over it, leaving xe_name_hash describing a name that is no longer there. Find the entry again by the name being set, matching the type as well. The copy carries every entry and every name over unchanged, and (type, name) pairs are unique within a block, so the match is exact. The type matters because the handlers strip their prefix before calling ocfs2_xattr_set(), so user.foo and trusted.foo share a stored name, a stored length and a hash, and both can sit in the same block. The name has to come from xi rather than from xs->here: a failed set can remove the entry xs->here names, and only the "growing" caller sets ctxt->set_abort, which is what stops the conversion. Scan every entry rather than narrowing on the hash the way ocfs2_find_xe_in_bucket() does, since an existing entry keeps the hash it was stored under, which a kernel that sign-extended the name bytes made different from the one computed now. An empty result means the entry did not survive the failed set and this has become an insert; leaving xs->here alone would keep it pointing into the block, which is rewritten as a tree root before the caller reads it again.

t: ocfs2: do not index before the entry array when dividing an empty bucket
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: do not index before the entry array when dividing an empty bucket ocfs2_divide_xattr_bucket() appends an empty bucket carrying a sentinel hash when the source bucket has no divide position, taking that hash from xh_entries[start - 1]. ocfs2_xattr_find_divide_pos() returns count when every entry shares one hash, and its loop does not run at all for count < 2, so an empty bucket comes back with start == count == 0 and the read is xh_entries[-1]. That is outside the __counted_by_le(xh_count) bounds of xh_entries[] and lands on the header, so the value picked up is xh_count | xh_free_start << 16. One above it is written into the new bucket's xh_entries[0] and committed, which leaves a bucket whose first hash does not follow the bucket before it. ocfs2_xattr_bucket_find() binary searches on xh_entries[0], so the broken key hides the range the sentinel was meant to cover: getxattr() answers -ENODATA for an attribute that is stored, and an insert can go to the wrong bucket and leave two copies of a name. The cross cluster divide hands the same value back as a tree record's e_cpos, which then claims a hash range it does not cover. Read xh_entries[0] instead. The branch is only reached when every entry shares one hash, so for a non-empty bucket it holds the same value, and for an empty one it is the slot that carries the bucket key. An empty bucket reaches the divide from ocfs2_check_xattr_bucket_collision(), which reports no collision for one, through ocfs2_add_new_xattr_bucket() and ocfs2_extend_xattr_bucket(). It does not take a failed set to get there: a divide that finds no position is itself what leaves an empty sentinel bucket behind, and a later extend can pick it as the target.

t: ocfs2/dlm: serialize migration MLE cleanup on failure
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/dlm: serialize migration MLE cleanup on failure A migration MLE has a base reference for the mastering answer and an in-use reference held by dlm_migrate_lockres(). The finishing assertion consumes the base reference, but migration failure drops it again without checking whether the assertion already consumed it. The target queues its migration worker before it acknowledges the ALL_DONE packet, so its finishing assertion can be handled while the sender still waits for the status. If the connection fails before the status arrives, dlm_send_one_lockres() returns an error for a migration that the target has already completed: Old-master sender Finishing assertion ----------------- ------------------- publish MLE; take in-use reference send ALL_DONE; wait for status take lookup reference unlink MLE put lookup and base references send returns a connection error put base reference again; free MLE put in-use reference; access freed MLE dlm_assert_master_handler() holds dlm->spinlock from the MLE lookup to the final puts, and it takes dlm->master_lock around the unlink and the puts. Decide under the same locks: if the MLE is already unhashed, the assertion consumed the base reference, so drop only the sender's in-use reference. Otherwise unlink it before consuming the base reference so a later assertion no longer finds it. An assertion that got there first has also made the target the owner and cleared DLM_LOCK_RES_MIGRATING. Treating the attempt as failed at that point would leave the lockres owned by the target while this node still holds the other nodes' locks and refmap bits, so it could neither be purged nor migrated again. Finish our side as a completed migration does instead: drop those locks under res->spinlock if the target still owns the lockres, and recalculate its usage. Use the same cleanup for the pre-send failure, the send failure and the target-death failure paths. The sender's in-use reference keeps the MLE alive until its final put outside the nested locks. Successful migration retains its existing in-use-only put. A target that has died cannot assert after the sender has seen its death. The o2net node-down callback runs before the DLM one; it disconnects the node and flushes the workqueue that runs the message handlers, so an assertion already received has been handled by the time the DLM removes the node from the domain map. A node that leaves the domain cleanly sends its exit message only after its assertions have been answered. Two windows of the hand-over itself are left as they are: the handler switches the owner and the sender drops the other nodes' locks moments later, and an assertion from a live target that arrives after the sender has given up still meets the owner check in the handler. Waiting for the target before giving up would only stretch the first window into the time in which recovery of the target can observe it. t: ocfs2: stop recovery before shutting down local allocators
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: stop recovery before shutting down local allocators Recovery completion needs the local allocators until it has finished reclaiming a failed node's allocation window and truncate log. During unmount, quota recovery is stopped first, but that leaves recovery_state at OCFS2_REC_QUOTA_DISABLED. New non-quota recovery can still start. ocfs2_truncate_log_shutdown() drains existing completion work and releases osb_tl_bh before ocfs2_recovery_exit() closes that publication path: Unmount Recovery ------- -------- stop quota recovery; disable quotas truncate_log_shutdown() flush existing completion work recover another failed node queue completion flush local log; release buffer complete_truncate_log_recovery() use released osb_tl_bh recovery_exit(): disable and drain An extra buffer reference alone would still let completion append new records after the final truncate-log flush. Split stopping and draining recovery from freeing its state. Stop all recovery producers and drain completion work before shutting down either local allocator. Keep recovery-state release at its existing later point, so its lifetime relative to other teardown users stays unchanged. The second stop at recovery_exit() is harmless once recovery is disabled. t: ocfs2/cluster: unlink socket containers before releasing resources
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/cluster: unlink socket containers before releasing resources A socket container's node and socket must remain alive while the container is on sock_containers. The debugfs formatter reads sc_node and sc_sock under o2net_debug_lock without taking their references, but sc_kref_release() releases both before taking that lock to unlink the container. With CONFIG_DEBUG_FS enabled, a synchronous sender can retain its last socket-container reference after o2net_disconnect_node() has detached the connection and flushed o2net_wq. The caller runs outside that workqueue. After the sender removes its configfs dependency, node removal can proceed without waiting for the sender's final sc_put(): Sender (final sc_put) Configfs rmdir Debugfs reader -------------------- -------------- -------------- o2nm_undepend_item() Drop node item refs o2nm_node_put() [node can be freed] sc_seq_show() Lock debug lock Read sc_node->nd_name Unlock debug lock sc_node = NULL o2net_debug_del_sc() The earlier socket release has a similar window. The container is still selectable while its socket has been released and sc_sock has not yet been cleared: Sender (final sc_put) Debugfs reader -------------------- -------------- sock_release(sc->sc_sock) [socket can be freed] sc_seq_show() Lock debug lock Read sc_sock->sk fields Unlock debug lock sc_sock = NULL ... o2net_debug_del_sc() Move o2net_debug_del_sc() before releasing either resource. Unlinking under the existing debug lock waits for an active formatter to finish and prevents later readers from selecting the container. This covers both socket fields and node fields, including nd_num in the stats formatter. KASAN report as below: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in string+0x42b/0x470 Read of size 1 at addr ffff88810f56fc90 by task python3/506 CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 506 Comm: python3 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc4-next-20260921-pmb-ocfs2-functional-v1+ #1 PREEMPT(lazy) Hardware name: QEMU Ubuntu 24.04 PC v2 (i440FX + PIIX, arch_caps fix, 1996), BIOS 1.16.3-debian-1.16.3-2 04/01/2014 Call Trace: <TASK> dump_stack_lvl+0x93/0xd0 print_report+0xce/0x630 kasan_report+0xe0/0x110 string+0x42b/0x470 vsnprintf+0x330/0x1110 seq_printf+0x1a8/0x260 sc_seq_show+0x604/0x9f0 seq_read_iter+0x480/0x1110 seq_read+0x362/0x5a0 full_proxy_read+0x11f/0x180 vfs_read+0x1a0/0xc20 ksys_read+0x111/0x200 do_syscall_64+0x114/0x620 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f (User register dump omitted.) </TASK> Allocated by task 497: kasan_save_stack+0x33/0x60 kasan_save_track+0x14/0x30 __kasan_kmalloc+0xaa/0xb0 __kmalloc_cache_noprof+0x28d/0x610 o2nm_node_group_make_item+0xea/0x1a0 configfs_mkdir+0x762/0xca0 vfs_mkdir+0x399/0x7e0 filename_mkdirat+0x129/0x450 __x64_sys_mkdir+0x70/0xa0 do_syscall_64+0x114/0x620 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f Freed by task 505: kasan_save_stack+0x33/0x60 kasan_save_track+0x14/0x30 kasan_save_free_info+0x3b/0x60 __kasan_slab_free+0x5f/0x80 kfree+0x308/0x580 config_item_cleanup+0x14b/0x230 config_item_put+0x79/0x90 sc_put+0x454/0x6e0 o2net_send_message_vec+0x63d/0x1560 o2net_send_message+0xa6/0xe0 validation_send_write+0x17f/0x1d0 full_proxy_write+0x11f/0x180 vfs_write+0x25a/0x1010 ksys_write+ ---truncated---

t: ocfs2: cache the mount context for dentry lock callbacks
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: cache the mount context for dentry lock callbacks ocfs2_drop_dentry_lock() drops the inode reference before releasing the DENTRY lock. This lets inode eviction release the local inode and open locks before a remote unlink can proceed past the DENTRY lock. A DLM callback can still arrive before the DENTRY lock has been dropped. ocfs2_get_dentry_osb() obtains the mount context through dl_inode->i_sb, which can access a freed inode when the downconvert thread drops the last inode reference in its post-unlock callback: Downconvert thread DLM callback thread ------------------ ------------------- ocfs2_process_blocked_lock() ocfs2_dentry_post_unlock() ocfs2_dentry_lock_put() ocfs2_drop_dentry_lock() iput(dl->dl_inode) [inode reclaimed after RCU] ocfs2_blocking_ast() ocfs2_get_dentry_osb() dl->dl_inode->i_sb ocfs2_simple_drop_lockres() Store the mount context in the DENTRY lock resource's l_priv field and use the default mount-context lookup. Recover the containing dentry lock with container_of(), as already done for refcount locks, and remove ocfs2_get_dentry_osb(). ocfs2_dismount_volume() shuts down the DLM before freeing the mount context, so callbacks can use it without accessing the inode. Preserve the existing iput-before-unlock order to avoid delaying local inode and open lock release until after the DENTRY lock is released.

t: xfs: fix temporary cursor leak in btree shift corruption paths
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: fix temporary cursor leak in btree shift corruption paths In xfs_btree_lshift and xfs_btree_rshift, when XFS_IS_CORRUPT detects an invalid firstrec/lastrec result after xfs_btree_dup_cursor has successfully allocated a temporary cursor, the error path jumps to error0 which returns without freeing tcur. This leaks the cursor memory, the xfs_group reference, and the per-level buffer references held by the duplicated cursor. Jump to error1 instead, which calls xfs_btree_del_cursor(tcur, XFS_BTREE_ERROR) to properly release all resources.

t: net/sched: sch_qfq: prevent aggregate self-replacement
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/sched: sch_qfq: prevent aggregate self-replacement qfq_change_class() snapshots the current aggregate settings while holding the qdisc tree lock, but drops the lock before selecting the destination aggregate. During that gap, qfq_enqueue() can move the class to an aggregate matching the requested settings. When qfq_change_class() resumes, qfq_find_agg() then returns cl->agg. If it is a singleton, qfq_deact_rm_from_agg() frees the aggregate before qfq_add_to_agg() immediately accesses the same pointer, causing a use-after-free. While holding the tree lock, skip the replacement when the destination is already the current aggregate. Any estimator replacement has already completed, so the class change can finish normally.

t: vhost-scsi: zero misaligned I/O bounce pages
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: vhost-scsi: zero misaligned I/O bounce pages The misaligned I/O fallback copies the full bounce scatterlist to the request buffer during completion. If a data-in command transfers less than requested, part of a newly allocated bounce page can remain unwritten. Allocate bounce pages with __GFP_ZERO so all bytes copied during completion have a defined value. This path is already the slow fallback for misaligned I/O, so the added initialization cost is acceptable. Found during an LLM-assisted source audit and validated with a QEMU/KVM vhost-scsi target using misaligned data-in commands.

t: vhost: fix used ring index wrap in vhost_add_used_n_in_order
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: vhost: fix used ring index wrap in vhost_add_used_n_in_order vhost_add_used_n_in_order() advances start by nheads[i] but wraps it with a single subtraction. If start + nheads[i] >= 2 * vq->num, start can remain outside the ring. With used-ring logging enabled, start > vq->num makes (vq->num - start) underflow. log_write() then sets bits beyond the dirty-log bitmap, potentially corrupting adjacent userspace memory. This is reachable on the vhost-net TX path with VIRTIO_F_IN_ORDER: done_idx can reach VHOST_NET_BATCH (64), triggering the issue with a 32-entry ring. Wrap start with a mask to keep it within the ring. VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM enforces a nonzero power-of-two ring size, allowing start to be wrapped using & (vq->num - 1).

t: iommu/virtio: Reset device before deleting virtqueues on probe failure
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommu/virtio: Reset device before deleting virtqueues on probe failure viommu_probe() marks the device DRIVER_OK before populating the event virtqueue and registering the IOMMU device in sysfs. viommu_fill_evtq() hands the device a set of device-writable buffers through virtqueue_add_inbuf(), so from that point on the device may write into them and into the rings. If either step fails, the error path deletes the virtqueues without resetting the device first. The event buffers are allocated with devm_kmalloc_array() and are released as probe unwinds, so the device can go on writing to memory that has been freed. Reset the device before deleting the virtqueues, the way viommu_remove() already does.

t: hwrng: virtio - prevent use-after-free after a failed restore
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: hwrng: virtio - prevent use-after-free after a failed restore remove_common() frees the driver data during freeze, but does not clear vdev->priv, which points to freed memory.
